**Employee Fired for Uninstalling App that Tracked Her Location**

A former sales executive at Intermex Wire Transfer LLC has filed a lawsuit against her ex-employer in Kern County Superior Court, alleging invasion of privacy, retaliation, and other labor code violations. Myrna Arias claims she was fired after uninstalling an app called Xora (now ClickSoftware Solution) on her company issued iPhone.

According to court documents, Arias' boss John Stubits asked employees to download StreetSmart web-based management application which enables office staff to track employee location 24/7 even when they are off-the-clock. The software also allows employers to see where their workers have been during work hours. 

The plaintiff's attorney Gail Glick said that this is not just about tracking worker locations but it is more than that; "They were treating her like a felon." She added that there is no legitimate business interest in monitoring employees outside working hours as long as they're doing nothing wrong.

Glick stated that Arias did well in her job earning around $7250 per month before being terminated by Intermex. However, everything changed when she refused to install the app citing concerns over invasion of privacy. According to the complaint, Arias researched the app and found out that it could be used to monitor employees’ whereabouts both while they’re on duty or off-duty. This made her feel uncomfortable because she felt like she was under constant surveillance.

In addition to wrongful termination, Arias alleges that Intermex’s president Robert Lisy intentionally interfered with her contract with NetSpend Corporation, leading them to fire her too. As a result, Arias now faces two black marks on her employment record and difficulty finding new jobs due to these issues.

Intermex has yet to comment on the matter.
details.ground_truth: Myrna Arias didn't like the GPS app on her phone that constantly tracked her, so she uninstalled it. The problem: Arias' iPhone was issued by her employer, which required her to run the app constantly, and after she removed it, the California woman was fired. Now she's suing her former employer, money transfer service Intermex, for invasion of privacy, unfair business practices, and retaliation, among other things, Ars Technica reports. Arias started researching the app, then called Xora—its website touts the app's ability to let employers "instantly see where their employees are and where they have been"—and eventually she and some of her colleagues asked a trainer from the app company to clarify. Boss John Stubits then, per the suit, "admitted that employees would be monitored while off duty and bragged that he knew how fast she was driving at specific moments." Arias says she has no problem being monitored while at work, but she complained to Stubits about being tracked in her free time; he was unsympathetic and said she should have no problem because of how much she was being paid by Intermex. "Her manager made it clear that he was using the program to continuously monitor her, during company as well as personal time," the complaint states, noting that he told Arias she needed to keep her phone on at all times in case a customer called. Arias' attorney tells Courthouse News that there was no way to turn the app off, as it would constantly run in the background. "She found it very offensive that they were treating her like a felon," the attorney says. Arias says her boss "scolded" her for uninstalling the program last year, and fired her soon after. **The Lovely Bones Movie Review**

Peter Jackson's adaptation of Alice Sebold's bestselling novel "The Lovely Bones" has been met with mixed reviews from critics and audiences alike. The film tells the story of Susie Salmon (Saoirse Ronan), a 14-year-old girl who is murdered by her neighbor George Harvey (Stanley Tucci). From heaven, Susie narrates her family's experience as they cope with their loss.

While Peter Jackson successfully recreates the eerie atmosphere of the book, he struggles to balance its tone, veering between sentimental warmth and serial-killer horror. Critics argue that this unevenness undermines the narrative, making it feel like a watered-down version of the original novel.

Despite these criticisms, Saoirse Ronan shines in the lead role, bringing depth and emotion to Susie's character. Her performance is particularly notable when she utters simple yet poignant lines about coping with death.

Other cast members also deliver strong performances, including Stanley Tucci as the chilling killer George Harvey and Mark Wahlberg as Susie's father Jack. Rachel Weisz plays Susie's mother Abigail, but some critics find her portrayal too sugary sweet.

One area where the movie falls short is in its depiction of sex and violence. While the book tackles mature themes such as rape and murder, the film shies away from explicit content, opting for more sanitized scenes instead.

Overall, while **The Lovely Bones** has its moments, it fails to live up to expectations due to its inconsistent tone and lack of depth. Despite this, fans of the novel may still appreciate the film's visual representation of Susie's afterlife, which features stunning CGI work.

details.ground_truth: NASA is going to the sun. More specifically, it's launching an unmanned probe next year that will travel closer to the star than any spacecraft has done previously. "It's a spacecraft loaded with technological breakthroughs that will solve many of the largest mysteries about our star," says Nicola Fox of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. In less scientific terms, per the Telegraph: "We will finally touch the sun." The nuts and bolts: The mission: The 10-foot probe will launch in July or August of 2018 and eventually get to within 3.7 million miles of the sun, about seven times closer than any previous spacecraft. Eventually, it will be whizzing around the sun at a speed of 450,000 miles per hour, reports CNN. The mission ends in 2025. Corona: The probe will actually fly into the outermost part of the sun's atmosphere, called the corona, per a mission overview at NASA that touts "humanity's first visit to a star." The heat: The probe will rely on a 4.5-inch-thick carbon-composite solar shield to help it withstand temperatures up to 2,550 degrees Fahrenheit, reports Orlando's WKMG. Instruments will remain at room temperature. The name: The probe's name has been changed to the Parker Solar Probe to honor astrophysicist Eugene Parker, who's credited with discovering solar wind. Parker, who turns 90 in June, is a professor emeritus at the University of Chicago, and the Guardian recounts that the theory he put forward in 1958 about a stream of charged particles flowing from the sun was once thought to be "crazy." A first: This is the first time NASA has named a mission after a living scientist. "I'm certainly greatly honored," said the man himself, per Space.com. Two puzzles: Scientists hope to better understand two things in particular: "How is the solar wind accelerated, and why is the ... corona so much hotter than the solar surface?" (It's 3 million degrees Fahrenheit vs. 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit.) Why it matters: Generally, solar storms are relatively harmless when they reach Earth, but these particle bursts occasionally wreak havoc on satellites and here on Earth, and they have the potential to be devastating. "The more we know about how these processes work, the better we can get at predicting when they will happen," writes Loren Grush at the Verge.

**Data Breach News Summary**

In recent weeks, two major retailers have fallen victim to significant data breaches that compromised sensitive customer information.

Neiman Marcus was hit by hackers as far back as July 2013, with the breach not being fully contained until January 5th. The company disclosed the theft of customer credit card numbers and other personal info in late December, but only after inquiries from journalists. Neiman has apologized for the delay and is offering free credit monitoring services to affected customers. While the exact number of victims remains unknown, it's believed to be significantly fewer than Target's estimated 40 million.

Target, on the other hand, suffered a massive breach during the holiday season, affecting over 100 million customers worldwide. A report from computer firm iSight reveals that the malware used in the attack was highly sophisticated and "new" to eCrime circles. The software, which originated in Eastern Europe or Russia, allowed hackers to scrape credit card details from point-of-sale systems at multiple locations across the US. This type of hacking technique is expected to become more common due to its effectiveness and low risk of detection.

A joint investigation between federal authorities and private investigators suggests that both Neiman Marcus and Target may have been targeted by the same group of international hackers operating out of Eastern Europe. State attorneys general are also looking into the matter, exploring potential connections between the two attacks.

The reports highlight concerns about the increasing sophistication of cybercrime operations and the need for greater vigilance among consumers and businesses alike. As these investigations continue, we can expect further revelations about the scope and perpetrators behind these high-profile hacks.
details.ground_truth: It looks like the hackers that hit Target had lots of other, well, targets. The Department of Homeland Security recently sent retailers and financial service companies a secret memo warning that the Target hit appeared to be part of a larger international campaign, the Wall Street Journal reports, an insight gleaned with the help of Dallas cybersecurity firm iSight Partners. Yesterday, iSight released its own report, saying that a virus it's calling KAPTOXA "has potentially infected a large number of retail information systems"—and noting that the "intrusion operators displayed innovation and a high degree of skill," particularly in terms of the "operational sophistication" of the hack. The Journal shares this feature by way of example: The virus focused on stealing data during the peak hours of 10am and 5pm; the data was housed in a Target server that the hackers later accessed. The virus attacks point-of-sale systems in a way that is "new to eCrime," subverting traditional efforts to protect consumer data, the report warns, according to NBC. Parts of the code, which is impervious to all known antivirus software, have been online since last spring. It's partly in Russian, which US officials think may indicate a link to organized crime in the former Soviet Union. The finding follows reports of similar breaches at Neiman Marcus. That breach had gone unnoticed since July, the New York Times reports today; Neiman's system was only fully secured Sunday.

**Archaeological Discoveries in Bulgaria Unveil Ancient History**

In recent years, archaeologists have made several significant discoveries at various sites along the Black Sea coast of Bulgaria, shedding new light on the region's rich history and cultural heritage.

One of the most remarkable finds is a 6th-century lead tube reliquary containing ashes from John the Apostle's grave, discovered by Bulgarian archaeologists during excavations at the Burgas Regional Museum site in 2014. The tiny relic, measuring less than an inch long, was found alongside other artifacts, including a Late Antiquity stone inscription and pottery fragments dating back to the Roman period. According to Milen Nikolov, Director of the Burgas Regional Museum, this discovery is "one of the most important" ever made at the museum.

The find has sparked interest among scholars due to its rarity – only 43 similar relics are known worldwide. Historians believe that pilgrims would collect such relics as proof of their devotion, often carrying them with them for protection or display in churches. In fact, another relic, believed to be St. Ivan Island (St. John) where the Byzantine Empire defeated the Crusaders in 1300 AD.

Another notable finding is a medieval seal bearing the image of Tsar Theodore Svetoslav, which dates back to the late 13th century AD. This artifact provides valuable insight into the political landscape of the time.

Additionally, researchers uncovered evidence of human habitation dating back to the Late Antiquity era, around 5-7th centuries AD. Excavation also revealed remains of ancient buildings, fortresses, and roads used by early Christians traveling between pilgrimage centers like Ephesus, Jerusalem, Rome, and Constantinople.

These findings demonstrate the significance of the area now occupied by modern-day Burgos (Poros), situated near Cape Foros, as a major hub connecting Europe and Asia through trade routes and Christian pilgrimage paths. Archaeologists continue to uncover more secrets about the past, providing a glimpse into the lives of people who lived there over two millennia ago.

Sources:

*   [Bulgarian National Radio](https://www.bnr.bg/en/news/2021/02/24/2241113)
*   [Ancient Origins](https://www.ancient-origins.net/)
*   [CNN](https://edition.cnn.com/)
details.ground_truth: Archaeologists in Bulgaria think they've found ashes belonging to one of the 12 apostles. The team found a small lead container with ashes while excavating a basilica that dates back to the sixth century AD, reports Archaeology in Bulgaria. The markings on the inch-long vessel match those at the grave of St. John the Apostle in what is now Turkey, leading researchers to surmise that a long-ago Christian from Bulgaria traveled to the grave site and returned home with the sample of ashes. Such journeys were common around that time, reports Novinite. “Probably a pilgrim from the Foros Peninsula went on a pilgrimage to Ephesus, and came back here with this relic, which was then donated to the basilica on Foros,” says the director of the Burgas Regional Museum of History in Bulgaria. (The ancient basilica is located in what is now the Black Sea city of Burgas.) Archeologists also found a Bulgarian royal seal from the 10th century at the dig site, which includes a fortress, notes the Week. (Another archaeological discovery: an ancient underground city in Turkey.)

**Netflix Introduces Unlimited Maternity and Paternity Leave Policy**

In a move to attract and retain top talent in the industry, Netflix has announced an unlimited maternity and paternity leave policy for its employees. The new program allows parents to take off as much time as they need during the first year after their child's birth or adoption, with no limit on paid leave.

According to Tawni Cranz, Chief Talent Officer at Netflix, the company wants to foster a "freedom and responsibility" culture that gives employees flexibility and confidence to balance work and family life without worrying about finances. Under this policy, parents can return part-time, full-time, or go back out as needed, while still receiving normal pay from the company.

This generous benefit is seen as a landmark perk by many experts, who note that it sets Netflix apart from other companies like Yahoo!, Facebook, and Google, which have also increased their parental leave policies in recent years. By offering such benefits, Netflix aims to compete for the best talent in the field and demonstrate its commitment to supporting employees' well-being outside of work.

While some may see unlimited time-off policies as having pitfalls, such as straining workplace relations or creating scheduling challenges, Netflix believes that providing flexible leave options will ultimately lead to more focused and dedicated employees when they do return to work.

The introduction of this policy comes just hours after Netflix hit its all-time stock price high, highlighting the importance of attracting and retaining top talent in today's competitive job market. With this bold step forward, Netflix solidifies its position as a leader in employee benefits and demonstrates its dedication to fostering a positive and supportive work environment.
details.ground_truth: Expecting parents wondering which company offers the best maternity and paternity leave in the US need look no further. The streaming video company based in Los Gatos, Calif., also offers unlimited paid vacation, and it's all toward fostering "a 'freedom and responsibility' culture that gives our employees context about our business and the freedom to make their own decisions along with the accompanying responsibility," writes Tawni Cranz, chief talent officer. The new policy "deserves high marks for extending leave to fathers," reports Fortune, "as well as understanding that the entire first year after childbirth can be challenging." It's a "landmark perk," reports TechCrunch, noting that Yahoo doubled its maternity and paternity leave in 2013 (to 16 paid weeks for moms and eight paid weeks for dads) to compete with packages offered by Facebook and Google because "the talent is growing up." A decade ago big company perks included free lunch and ping pong tables, but now the major moves are about helping employees balance work and home life because "experience shows people perform better at work when they’re not worrying about home," Cranz adds. Of course, employees will have to plan their leave with managers and coworkers in advance to make sure their absence isn't disruptive—behaving, you know, like adults. Two recent incidents have highlighted concerns about racism and antisemitism in universities.

In London, an investigation is underway at the London School of Economics (LSE) after allegations emerged that a Nazi-themed drinking game led to a brawl involving a Jewish student's broken nose during a skiing trip organized by the students' union last month. The game involved playing cards arranged in the shape of a swastika and players were required to "salute the Führer". A Jewish society representative described the incident as a "spiteful, collective attack" on the community.

The LSE has condemned the alleged behavior, stating that it does not tolerate antisemitism or any other form of racism. An inquiry into the matter is ongoing, with disciplinary action possible if the allegations are proven true.

This incident follows another reported case from November 2022, where members of Oxford University Conservative Association allegedly sang an antisemitic song with Nazi references.

These cases raise questions about the prevalence of racist and antisemitic attitudes among university students and whether enough is being done to address these issues. Many universities pride themselves on promoting diversity and inclusivity, but these incidents suggest that more work needs to be done to create safe spaces for all students.

Experts warn that such behaviors can have serious consequences, including physical harm and emotional distress for those targeted. They also highlight the need for greater awareness and education about the impact of hate speech and discriminatory actions.

As institutions strive to promote tolerance and respect, they must take concrete steps to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future. This includes providing training programs for students and staff, implementing robust reporting mechanisms, and taking swift action against perpetrators of hate crimes.

**Multiple Robberies and Shooting in Kansas City Area**

A series of robberies and shootings has shaken the community in Kansas City, Missouri, after two separate incidents occurred within hours of each other on Wednesday night.

The first incident took place at approximately 7pm when a couple was shot while attempting to purchase their teenage son's car from an individual they met through Craigslist. The suspects fled with $3,000 cash that was left inside the vehicle. A short time later, around 8 pm, another family reported being robbed by four individuals who were also using Craigslist for the sale. In this case, however, the father shielded his child as bullets flew past him during the attack. He suffered multiple gunshot wounds but is recovering well following surgery.

Police are investigating both cases and have identified several persons of interest in connection with these crimes. They remain at large. Anyone with information can contact TIPS Hotline or Crime Stoppers. 

In total, three people were injured including the man who received four gunshots and woman whose arm shattered due to gunfire. Their teenager remained unharmed throughout the ordeal. Witnesses described seeing bystanders fail to provide assistance despite hearing screams for help.

As police continue searching for those responsible, Ferrellgas company increased its reward donation to $5,000 towards catching them. This brings the overall reward up to $7,000.
details.ground_truth: A Kansas City couple who went to check out a car they saw on Craigslist were shot and robbed Wednesday night, USA Today reports. They had wanted to purchase the vehicle for their 16-year-old son, who was with them but not injured. Police say the 53-year-old dad and his son had test-driven a 2007 Hyundai Sonata and were discussing payment when the seller said he had to call his wife and momentarily walked away, according to KCTV. That’s when two other men reportedly approached the family and demanded cash, then started shooting. As the dad tried to keep his wife and son out of the barrage of bullets, he was shot four times in the chest, stomach, and legs, while his 55-year-old wife took a bullet to her upper right arm, which was “shattered,” reports the TV station. The men took the wife's purse, which had $3,000 in cash for the car purchase, say police. Authorities believe the incident may be related to an earlier armed robbery that day in which a Kansas City man says he tried to sell his Xbox and gaming accessories to a man who saw his ad on Craigslist, reports the Kansas City Star. As the potential buyer was examining the wares, two other men reportedly arrived sporting a gun; the three men then lifted the Xbox and other items and ran into nearby woods, police say.

**Data Brokers Exposed for Selling Sensitive Consumer Information**

A recent Senate Commerce Committee report has shed light on the multibillion-dollar data industry's practices, revealing that major companies are selling deeply personal and sensitive information about consumers to marketers without their consent.

The investigation found that nine leading data brokers, including Acxiom, Equifax, and Spokeo, have amassed vast amounts of consumer profiles containing intimate details such as medical conditions, financial history, and even lists of rape victims. These companies claim they sell this information to help businesses target specific audiences, but critics argue it puts individuals at risk of identity theft, harassment, or exploitation.

Some disturbing examples include:

*   Data broker Epsilon selling lists of people with cancer, HIV/AIDS, and other serious health issues.
*   Another company offering "Rape Victims" and "Sex Offenders" lists for sale.
*   A third firm providing access to home addresses and phone numbers of police officers and firefighters.

While some data brokers cooperated with the committee's inquiry, others refused to provide information or were unresponsive. The lack of transparency is particularly concerning given that many consumers remain unaware of what data is being collected about them and how it is used.

In response to these findings, lawmakers are calling for increased regulation of the data brokerage industry. Senator John Rockefeller (D-WV) criticized several large data brokers for resisting oversight and vowed to continue pushing for greater accountability.

"This is where I urge Congress to take action," said Pam Dixon, executive director of the World Privacy Forum. "We need stronger laws in place to protect individual privacy."

As concerns grow over the misuse of consumer data, experts warn that more needs to be done to safeguard Americans' rights and prevent further exploitation by data brokers.
details.ground_truth: Secretive data companies are tracking almost every American's every move online—and compiling and selling disturbingly targeted lists based on that spying, a new Senate Commerce Committee report concludes. That includes lists of rape victims, people suffering from ailments including HIV, AIDS, and dementia, and people with substance abuse problems, a privacy group said in a hearing yesterday, as per CNN. Mailing addresses for police officers and domestic violence shelters—the latter of which are usually protected by law—are also for sale, as are lists based on demographics and economics, including "Ethnic Second-City Strugglers," and "Rural and Barely Making It." The World Privacy Forum urged Congress to act to "remove unsafe, unfair, and overall just deplorable lists from circulation." The Direct Marketing Association released a statement saying that while the lists are occasionally "used to disparage certain groups," they represented a "tiny minority" of marketing products. Overall the committee looked at nine companies, some of which refused to explain how they got their data or who they sold it to, Gawker reports. One company admitted it had sold social security numbers and banking information to an alleged identity theft ring.

**Libya's Ongoing Humanitarian Crisis Deepens as Rebels Search for Gaddafi**

The situation in Libya continues to deteriorate as rebels search for Moammar Gaddafi and his loyalists. Thousands of people remain missing after peaceful protests against Gaddafi turned into an armed conflict that has left nearly 60,000 dead.

A young rebel fighter, Faraj, had lost hope when he disappeared on the front lines in March. His family feared the worst, but were overjoyed when he was reunited with them last Sunday at Tripoli airport. Abdul Rauf, another detainee who spent 48 days in Abu Salim prison, shared similar stories of torture and abuse by pro-Gaddafi forces.

However, not everyone is so fortunate. Muneer Masoud Own, 33, barely escaped from a warehouse where dozens of prisoners were slaughtered by pro-Gaddafi forces as rebels closed in on Tripoli last week. The charred remains of at least 150 bodies have been found inside the warehouse, while others are believed to be buried under piles of earth nearby.

Rebel leaders estimate that up to 60,000 Libyans may still be missing since the start of the uprising, including many held in secret prisons like Abu Salim. Families of those detained continue to wait anxiously for any information about their loved ones' fate.

As the humanitarian crisis deepens, volunteers are working tirelessly to identify victims and provide aid to affected families. But without access to official records or clear evidence, it will take time before we know the full extent of the tragedy unfolding in Libya.

In related developments, Libyan officials say they have freed thousands of detainees from Gaddafi's notorious prisons, but only around 10% of these individuals can be accounted for. Rebel leader Shamsiddin said "Where are they?" referring to the estimated tens of thousands of missing persons.

Meanwhile, residents near the site of the massacre described scenes of unimaginable horror, with some reporting seeing guards shoot detainees point-blank in the head. Others spoke of being forced to endure extreme conditions, such as no food or water, in cramped warehouses filled with human waste.

These accounts paint a grim picture of life under Gaddafi's rule, which appears to have descended further into chaos and brutality as the regime teeters on collapse. As international pressure mounts for accountability, hopes rise among Libyans that justice will eventually prevail.
details.ground_truth: Troops loyal to Moammar Gadhafi massacred some 150 detainees last week, according to volunteers who cleared charred bodies from the warehouse that had apparently served as the detainees’ prison. An escaped prisoner told his story to CNN: He and his brother were handcuffed and blindfolded for no apparent reason while out walking earlier this month. They were thrown into the warehouse with 60 others ages 17 to 70. The number inside quickly reached 175 as loyalists continued to imprison people. The detainees were given no food or water for days, said Muneer Own. Finally, the troops said they would set them free—but instead hurled a grenade at them and opened fire. About 25 people were able to escape, Own said; his brother apparently was not one of them. The mass of bodies was discovered when rebels eventually took over the area. Many remain unidentified, part of a growing number of prisoners whose whereabouts remain unknown, notes the Washington Post. Thousands—some of whom have been jailed for decades—could be in underground prisons or mass graves, rebels fear. Click through for one family’s story.

**Yo-Yo Dieting Linked to Increased Risk of Heart Attacks and Strokes in People with Coronary Artery Disease**

A recent study published in The New England Journal of Medicine has found that rapidly losing and gaining weight (yo-yo dieting) may increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and death in people with coronary artery disease.

The study followed 9,509 men and women with stable coronary artery disease for five years, monitoring their weight fluctuations over time. Researchers found that those who experienced significant weight changes had an increased risk of:

* 78% higher risk of new-onset diabetes
* 124% higher risk of deaths
* 117% higher risk of heart attacks
* 136% higher risk of strokes

Coronary artery disease is caused by the buildup of cholesterol-rich plaque on the inner walls of arteries, leading to reduced blood flow to the heart. This can cause chest pain, shortness of breath, and even heart failure if left untreated.

According to Mayo Clinic, coronary artery disease develops when inflammation causes damage to the inner lining of the arteries, allowing fatty deposits to accumulate. A healthy lifestyle, including regular exercise, balanced diet, and stress management, can help prevent or manage this condition.

Previous studies have also linked yo-yo dieting to poor cardiovascular health outcomes. However, researchers from NYU Langone Medical Center's Cardiovascular Clinical Research Center took it a step further by examining the impact of weight fluctuation specifically among individuals with pre-existing coronary heart disease.

Their findings suggest that large weight swings are associated with significantly worse outcomes, including more frequent heart attacks, strokes, and mortality rates. Specifically, they discovered that participants experiencing the largest weight fluctuations were at a staggering 124% greater risk of dying compared to those whose weights remained relatively steady.

While these results raise concerns about the potential risks of yo-yo dieting, lead author Dr. Sripal Bangalore emphasizes that maintaining a consistent body weight through sustainable lifestyle habits remains crucial for overall well-being.

"We need to be concerned about weight fluctuation in this group already at high risk," he said. "Our analysis suggests we should focus on helping Americans keep weight off rather than just focusing on rapid weight loss."

In conclusion, while the exact mechanisms behind the link between yo-yo dieting and adverse cardiac events remain unclear, research highlights the importance of adopting long-term strategies for managing weight and reducing cardiovascular risk factors. By prioritizing sustained lifestyle modifications, individuals with coronary artery disease can mitigate their chances of developing life-threatening complications.
details.ground_truth: Losing weight is one thing, keeping it off quite another. And now researchers are finding that among those with coronary heart disease (CHD)—which the Mayo Clinic reports develops from damaged or diseased blood vessels typically caused by blockage and inflammation—yo-yo dieting may dramatically increase the risk of stroke, heart attack, and death. Reporting in the New England Journal of Medicine, researchers say they followed nearly 10,000 men and women with CHD between the ages of 35 and 75 for about five years, monitoring changes in body weight and other health outcomes. The takeaway? "It's important to lose weight, but this data says you have to keep it off," lead researcher Dr. Sripal Bangalore at the New York University School of Medicine tells the New York Times. The highest weight fluctuation was on average 8.6 pounds over five years, while the smallest body weight changes averaged closer to two pounds, reports Medical News Today. Those who were already overweight or obese at the beginning of the study and who experienced the highest level of weight fluctuation experienced 124% more deaths, 136% more strokes, and 117% more heart attacks, meaning these CHD patients were more than twice as likely to suffer these negative outcomes in just a few years than people with CHD whose weight only fluctuated two pounds. This doesn't pinpoint a cause, as pre-existing heart problems could be the culprit, but researchers hope to study this correlation further. (Yo-yo dieting is bad for women's hearts in general.)

**Funeral Home Thief Steals Wedding Ring from Deceased Woman**

A shocking incident has occurred at Sunset Memorial Gardens & Funeral Home in Odessa, Texas, where an unidentified woman stole a wedding ring from a deceased person's body on April 8th.

According to police and family members, the thief entered the funeral home around 5:27 p.m., asking for directions to the restroom but instead making her way to the casket containing Lois Hicks' body. The suspect then yanked off the wedding ring from Hicks' left hand, tearing part of the skin in the process.

The theft was caught on video surveillance, which shows the suspect parking her vehicle outside, entering the building, and committing the crime before fleeing with the jewelry. The footage also captures several shots of the license plate number, which can be enhanced for closer examination.

Lois Hicks' daughter, Vel McKee, described the scene as "heartbreaking" and expressed shock that such a brazen act could occur against someone so defenseless. "I just never dreamed something like this would happen," she said.

Police are urging anyone with information about the identity or whereabouts of the suspect to come forward. A reward is being offered through Odessa Crime Stoppers (432-333-TIPS), and those who have any tips can contact them directly.

This incident marks a rare occurrence at Sunset Funeral Home, according to General Manager Bill Vallie, who stated it's the first time such a theft has happened since the facility opened its doors in 1999.

As authorities continue their investigation, they ask anyone with knowledge about the case to step forward and help bring justice to the Hicks family.
details.ground_truth: A Texas woman was caught on surveillance video stealing a wedding ring off the finger of a dead woman Friday, the Odessa American reports. The body of Lois Hicks, 88, was in an open casket at Odessa's Sunset Funeral Home. The woman's family had just left the funeral home after a visitation service when a stranger parked outside, came in, and asked to use the restroom. Instead, the funeral home's manager says, she walked into the room with Hicks' coffin, grabbed the ring off her finger, and left. Hicks' daughter says some of her mother's skin was actually torn off during the theft. "I can't believe someone would be that low," she says. The surveillance video captured the alleged thief's license plate, and the family is pressing charges. The incident is being investigated as a felony, KOSA reports. The suspect is described as a heavy-set white woman who was wearing a brown long-sleeved sweater, black sweat pants, and black sandals at the time; she drove off in a red or maroon four-door Saturn.

**Tragedy at Hawaii Dentist's Office: 3-Year-Old Girl Dies After Dental Procedure**

A devastating incident has shaken the community in Kailua, Hawaii, after a 3-year-old girl named Finley Puleo Boyle died following a dental procedure at Island Dentistry for Children on December 3, 2013.

According to an autopsy report released by Honolulu Chief Medical Examiner Dr. Christopher Happy, Finley likely suffered from cardiac arrest due to the sedatives and local anesthesia administered during her visit. The medical examiner classified the death as an accident.

Finley had been scheduled to undergo four root canals but was given five different drugs, including Demerol, hydroxyzine, chlorohydrate, laughing gas, and lidocaine with epinephrine. Immediately after receiving the lidocaine injection, she became unresponsive and went into cardiopulmonary arrest.

The family of Finley filed a negligence lawsuit against Dr. Lilly Geyer, who owns Island Dentistry for Children. According to court documents, the technician administering the medication did not monitor Finley's oxygen levels every five minutes, instead waiting 26 minutes before checking them again. Additionally, no CPR was performed until someone retrieved a doctor from another office.

Despite these allegations, the medical examiner's office ultimately ruled the death an accident. No criminal charges have been brought against Dr. Geyer or any staff members involved.

In response to this tragedy, new state rules took effect in January tightening oversight of dental sedation in Hawaii. These regulations aim to prevent similar incidents in the future.

Dr. Geyer's attorney, John Nishimoto, declined to comment further on the matter due to ongoing litigation. Rick Fried, the lawyer representing Finley's parents, also refused to discuss the details of the case.

This heartbreaking incident serves as a reminder of the importance of proper monitoring and care when using sedatives and anesthesia in medical procedures, particularly among vulnerable populations such as children. As investigations continue, it is essential that lessons are learned to ensure the safety of patients undergoing similar treatments.
details.ground_truth: Drugs are likely to blame for the death of Finley Boyle, the 3-year-old Hawaii girl who died a month after going into cardiac arrest during a root canal at a Kailua dentist's office on Dec. 3, according to the official autopsy report. The report says the combination of sedatives and anesthesia Finley received during the procedure probably caused her death, the AP reports. The report noted that Finley was healthy, and ruled out any signs of an underlying heart condition or an allergic reaction. The medical examiner's office ruled the toddler's death an accident, and no charges have been brought against Dr. Lilly Geyer, KHON reports; however, Finley's family has filed a lawsuit claiming Finley was not monitored for 26 minutes while she was under sedation. Geyer's office has since shut down, but Geyer's attorney calls the Boyle family's allegations "unproven." (Meanwhile, a young mother in Hawaii is in a coma following wisdom teeth surgery.)

**Hurricane Katrina's 10th Anniversary: Remembering Robert Ricks' Dire Forecast**

Ten years ago today, Hurricane Katrina made landfall in Louisiana, causing unprecedented destruction and devastation to New Orleans and surrounding areas. As we reflect on this tragic event, we remember the crucial role that National Weather Service meteorologist Robert Ricks played in warning residents about the impending disaster.

Ricks, who was working at the Slidell office outside New Orleans, issued an extraordinary bulletin just hours before the storm hit. The document, titled "URGENT... SPECIAL MESSAGE," warned of a powerful hurricane with unprecedented strength, predicting widespread damage and human suffering. Specifically, it stated that:

* Most of the area would be uninhabitable for weeks or longer.
* At least half of well-constructed homes would have roof and wall failure.
* Gabled roofs would fail entirely.
* Native trees would be snapped or uprooted.
* Water shortages would lead to incredible human suffering by modern standards.

This bold forecast, which has been hailed as one of the most dire ever issued by the National Weather Service, was not taken lightly by Ricks. In fact, he said that if he had known the extent of the damage, he would rather have been wrong than issue such a stark warning. However, his local expertise and experience from previous storms like Betsy and Camille led him to believe that this was indeed the big one.

As the city prepared for the worst, evacuations were underway, and people began arriving at the Superdome seeking shelter. Unfortunately, many did not heed the warnings, leading to catastrophic consequences when the storm struck.

Today, Ricks is back at work alongside colleagues who lost their homes during the disaster. He remains haunted by the response to the crisis, saying that it broke his heart because they always prepare for the big one – but never thought it would come so soon.

The legacy of Robert Ricks' dire forecast serves as a reminder of the importance of accurate and timely weather forecasting, particularly during times of true emergency. His bravery and dedication to public service will forever be remembered as a testament to the power of science and communication in saving lives.
details.ground_truth: It's one of the most famous weather forecasts of the modern era, and it came out exactly 13 years ago to the day. That would be Aug. 28, 2005, one day before Hurricane Katrina devastated New Orleans. National Weather Service meteorologist Robert Ricks issued a forecast so dire that some news agencies thought it was a hoax, writes meteorologist James Spann in a tweet commemorating the Ricks forecast. As it turns out, Ricks was spot on. "Most of the area will be uninhabitable for weeks…perhaps longer," he wrote. "At least one half of well constructed homes will have roof and wall failure. All gabled roofs will fail…leaving those homes severely damaged or destroyed." And this: "Water shortages will make human suffering incredible by modern standards." (Spann's tweet includes the full text.) The forecast has been credited with saving lives, and it is now in the Smithsonian Museum of American History, as noted by Slate on the 10-year anniversary. Ricks told Brian Williams of NBC News on Sept. 15, 2005, that he went through the warning line by line to verify each doomsday-sounding statement before making it public. He ended up removing nothing. "I would much rather have been wrong in this one," he told Williams. "I would much rather be talking to you and taking the heat and crying wolf. But our local expertise said otherwise. You know, 'Hey, let's gear up for the big one, this is going to be the big one.'" **Tragic Accident at Fleming Athletic Complex**

A 12-year-old boy, Melquan Kwame Robinson, died on Monday after being electrocuted while practicing football at Fleming Athletic Complex near Bernie Ward Community Center in Augusta, Georgia. According to Richmond County Coroner Mark Bowen, three other people were also injured during the incident.

The accident occurred when Melquan touched an electrified fence while trying to retrieve a ball that had gone over the chain link fence. Three others who attempted to save him suffered injuries and are currently recovering in hospital.

Melquan's family is still reeling from his sudden loss, with friends and teammates describing him as energetic, passionate about sports, and loved by everyone around him. His former coach Don Clark praised Melquan for his dedication to football and described him as "a future leader."

An investigation into the cause of the accident has been launched by local authorities, including the city, sheriff's office, and Georgia Power. The company released a statement expressing condolences to the families affected and promising cooperation with investigators.

As the community mourns the loss of this young life, parents and coaches have expressed their shock and sadness at the tragic event. A vigil will be held Thursday evening at Bernie Ward Community Center to honor Melquan's memory and support those grieving.

**Woman Impersonates Target Employee to Steal iPhones**

A woman has been identified as a suspect in a brazen theft at a Target store in Alexandria, Virginia. According to Fairfax County police, she impersonated an employee and stole over $40,000 worth of iPhones from the 6600 Richmond Highway location on March 15.

The thief was familiar with store procedures, including employee hours and where iPhones were kept in the stockroom. She gained access to the stockroom by pretending to be an employee and then loaded the stolen phones into a box before leaving the store.

Police describe the suspect as someone who is not affiliated with the store but appeared to have knowledge of its inner workings. The investigation is ongoing, and authorities urge anyone with tips or leads to contact them at (703) 691-2131.

This incident highlights the growing concern of retail crime and the need for increased security measures in stores across the country. As retailers continue to adapt to new technologies and shopping habits, they must also stay vigilant against sophisticated thieves like this suspect.

South Korea conducted live-fire drills off its east coast in response to the nuclear test, while Japan and China have called for restraint from both sides.

Russia's Vladimir Putin has urged calm, saying that diplomacy should prevail over military action. He also criticized the US for conducting joint military exercises with South Korea, stating that they will only increase tensions.

China's Xi Jinping reiterated calls for global peace during his visit to Russia ahead of the economic summit in Vladivostok.

It appears unlikely that North Korea will launch another ICBM soon, given their preference for timing major events to coincide with significant world headlines.

Meanwhile, the White House tells Reuters it has given "in-principle approval" to a request by South Korean President Moon Jae-in to abolish a limit regarding warhead weights, a move that would strengthen the power with which it could attack the North, if necessary. Meanwhile, Vladimir Putin on Tuesday gave his take on the situation: North Korea "will eat grass but will not give up the (nuclear) program if they don't feel safe."

**Tragic Accident Claims Life of 6-year-old Boy in Texas**

A devastating incident occurred on Thursday when six-year-old Kameron Prescott was fatally shot by deputies during a manhunt for a suspect at his family's mobile home park in Schertz, Texas. The Bexar County Sheriff's Office has confirmed that four deputies were involved in the shooting.

According to authorities, Amanda Lene Jones, a 30-year-old woman with multiple felony arrests, had stolen a vehicle and led law enforcement on a two-hour chase before being cornered outside Kameron's residence. Deputies believed she posed an imminent threat and opened fire, striking both Jones and Kameron.

Sheriff Javier Salazar described the incident as a "tragic accident" and stated that policies appear to have been followed. However, he acknowledged that it is heartbreaking video footage captured from body cameras worn by the officers shows the moment they fired their guns.

Kameron, who attended Wiederstein Elementary School, was remembered by teachers and classmates as a kind-hearted boy with a contagious smile. His first-grade teacher, Shanda Ince, said he loved making everyone laugh and would be deeply missed.

The investigation into the shooting continues, but officials are still searching for evidence of a handgun allegedly wielded by Jones. A dark-colored pipe found near her body contained bloodstains matching hers, according to investigators.

In response to this tragedy, the school district established a memorial fund to support Kameron's family with expenses. Donations can be made through local banks or mailed to:

Kameron Prescott Memorial Fund

As the community mourns the loss of young Kameron, many wonder what could have been done differently to prevent such a tragic outcome. For now, residents remain shaken by the senseless killing of an innocent child caught up in a chaotic situation involving desperate individuals.
details.ground_truth: Sheriff's deputies shot and killed a 6-year-old boy Thursday in Texas, WOAI reports. Bexar County Sheriff Javier Salazar says four deputies opened fire on 30-year-old Amanda Jones, a suspected car thief, after they "cornered" her outside a mobile home occupied by Kameron Prescott and his family in the town of Schertz. One of the bullets went through the mobile home and hit Kameron in the abdomen. According to CNN, Salazar says deputies performed first aid on the boy, but he was pronounced dead at the hospital. Jones was also killed. "The deputies are, of course, understandably shaken up," Salazar says. He says the shooting is under investigation, but in his opinion the boy's death is "a tragic accident." Salazar says one deputy is "adamant" he saw Jones with a gun and that she threatened to shoot him. He says Jones threatened both police and Kameron's family, who didn't know her, just before deputies opened fire. But investigators haven't been able to locate a gun despite the use of a helicopter and dive team. Salazar says they have found a pipe with Jones' blood on it near the scene of the shooting. One deputy at the scene was wearing a body camera, but he blocked it with his rifle during the shooting. Meanwhile, Kameron is being remembered by those who knew him. "Kameron was a ball of energy, happy, smart, and could strike up a conversation with anyone,” school counselor Maria Morales tells KSAT. “He also had a great sense of humor and caring heart."

**Vegan Mother Arrested for Neglecting Newborn Son**

A Seminole County mother has been arrested and charged with child neglect after allegedly refusing to seek medical attention for her dehydrated newborn son due to her vegan lifestyle.

Sarah Anne Markham was taken into custody on Tuesday after police received a tip about the situation through the Florida Child Abuse Hotline. According to authorities, Markham's 2-week-old baby boy, Caleb, had lost weight and was diagnosed as severely dehydrated by doctors at the hospital.

Markham claimed that she did not want to give her son formula made from animal products, which is standard practice in infant care. Instead, she wanted to use soy-based formula, despite warnings from healthcare professionals that this could be detrimental to his health.

The case first came to light in June when Markham's husband reported concerns about their son's rapid weight loss. A doctor ordered an emergency visit to the hospital, but Markham refused to take her son there, citing her vegan beliefs. The couple's grandparents eventually took custody of the baby, who now weighs 17 pounds and appears healthy.

Markham was released on bond later that day and claims that she will continue to fight for custody of her son. Her attorney, Mark O'Mara, expects the charges against her to be dropped, stating "There's no abuse, there's no neglect – just a challenged mom."

However, prosecutors argue that Markham's actions put her child's life at risk and demonstrate a clear disregard for expert advice. If convicted, Markham faces up to five years in prison.

**Colorectal Cancer on the Rise Among Younger Adults**

A recent study has found that colorectal cancer is increasingly being diagnosed in people under 50 years old, challenging traditional guidelines for screening and treatment. According to data from the University of Michigan and other researchers, nearly 15% of colon cancer cases are now occurring among individuals younger than 50.

The analysis of over 258,000 patients with colorectal cancer revealed that:

* One in seven colon cancers are now diagnosed in people under 50.
* By 2030, this number is expected to rise to one in four (25%) due to an estimated increase in incidence rates.
* Despite more aggressive treatments, young adults tend to live slightly longer after diagnosis compared to their older counterparts.
* The reasons behind this trend remain unclear, but experts speculate that environmental factors such as diet, lifestyle choices like smoking or obesity may be contributing to the rising numbers.

Researchers emphasize that these findings should serve as a "wake-up call" for healthcare professionals to consider alternative approaches to early detection and prevention. However, some experts caution against expanding screening guidelines without further research, citing concerns about potential harm caused by unnecessary screenings.

Dr. Samantha Hendren, lead author of the study, notes that while there's no clear evidence yet supporting changes to current guidelines, it's essential to prepare for the increasing number of very young survivors who will require long-term support.

In response to these findings, Dr. David Weinberg suggests considering family history, genetic predisposition, and symptoms when deciding whether to screen younger patients. He also highlights the importance of addressing modifiable risk factors through education and public health initiatives.

As the medical community grapples with these new statistics, ongoing studies aim to shed light on the underlying causes driving this alarming trend. For now, awareness campaigns focus on recognizing warning signs – including rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, and unexplained weight loss – which can prompt earlier intervention and potentially save lives.

- Abdelsattar et al., Colorectal Cancer Outcomes in Patients Under Age 50 (2016)
- Reuters Health, Colon Cancers Rising in People Under 50 (January 26, 2016)

details.ground_truth: A new study says one in seven US colon cancer patients is younger than 50—raising questions about why more young people seem to be getting the disease and what can be done about it, reports HealthDay via the Philadelphia Inquirer. "Colon cancer has traditionally been thought of as a disease of the elderly," says lead author Samantha Hendren. "This study is really a wake-up call to the medical community that a relatively large number of colon cancers are occurring in people under 50." Using government data on almost 260,000 colon-cancer patients from 1998 to 2011, the study also says younger patients more often have advanced cancer and undergo surgery (72% compared to 63% of patients over 50). The young are also more likely to use radiation therapy (53% to 48%) and have a slight advantage in surviving for five years (68% to 67%). Younger people are more likely to have advanced colon cancer partly because they get tested after noticing symptoms (like colon blockage, bleeding, and anemia), while people over 50 are advised to begin screenings, says Hendren. "Unfortunately, these symptoms are often ignored by the patient or doctor or ascribed to something like hemorrhoids," a scientist adds, per Reuters. Hendren's team conducted the study after noticing a rise in colon cancer among young people, Medical Daily reports, but that spike remains unexplained. Physical inactivity, obesity, smoking, and "an effect in our environment" are all possible causes, a Harvard professor says. More screenings for young people might help, but the yield would be low because under-50s are still less likely to get colon cancer. "This would be a big and costly change," says Hendren, who recommends "a lot of research" be done first. (A new killer is expected to top cancer by 2050.)

details.ground_truth: "A man getting out of the car to go to the toilet led to the discovery of one of the most important sites in Australian pre-history," archaeologist Giles Hamm tells ABC News. Hamm was surveying a section of Australia's Flinders Ranges when his partner, aboriginal elder Clifford Coulthard, had to go to the bathroom. "Nature called and Cliff walked up this creek bed into this gorge and found this amazing spring surrounded by rock art," Hamm says. At the time, Hamm thought the newly discovered human settlement, a site called Warratyi, was only 5,000 years old. It turns out it's closer to 49,000 years old, and that has huge ramifications for our knowledge of ancient Australian civilization, Sky News reports. Hamm and his team published a study on Warratyi this week in Nature. The discovery of Warratyi in the arid interior of the continent means humans either arrived in Australia up to 10,000 years earlier than previously believed—or they expanded across the continent at a much quicker rate, Science Alert reports. Researchers at the site found 4,300 objects, including tools, and 200 bone fragments from multiple animals, including a 5,500-pound marsupial. The bones help explain how early Australians interacted with megafauna, including hunting them. The tools show Australians were using bone and stone axes earlier than believed and are evidence that early Australians developed some technologies on their own rather than adopting them from other peoples as previously believed. (Ninety rocks in Australia could rank up there with Stonehenge.)

**Snap's Spectacles Now Available for Purchase Online**

After generating significant buzz and demand through its limited release strategy, Snap Inc.'s camera-enabled sunglasses, Spectacles, are now available for purchase online in the United States.

The $130 glasses, which allow wearers to take circular videos that can be posted directly to Snapchat accounts, were previously only sold through vending machines that popped up in surprise locations around the country or at a store in Manhattan. The scarcity of these devices led to high resale prices on eBay, with some pairs selling for as much as $5,000.

However, starting today, users can buy Spectacles from the company's website (Spectacles.com) without having to wait in line or track down a roving vending machine. The glasses come in three colors - teal, coral, and black - and will ship within two to four weeks. A six-pair limit per household has been implemented to prevent bulk purchases.

This move is seen as an effort by Snap to prove to investors that Spectacles can generate revenue beyond just being a brand stunt. While the device has received positive feedback since its launch last November, it has not yet generated significant sales for the company. In fact, according to Snap's SEC filing, the company lost $514.6 million last year, highlighting the need for Spectacles to contribute meaningfully to their bottom line.

To put this into perspective, if Snap sells approximately 4 million pairs of Spectacles this year, they would break even based on their reported losses. This milestone could help bolster confidence in the company ahead of its initial public offering.

In addition to online sales, pop-up vending machines will continue to appear in various locations across the US, although they may take a short "nap" before resuming operations. With the expanded availability of Spectacles, fans of the product should have easier access to purchasing them, but those looking to snag a pair quickly might still face competition from eager buyers.

A total of seven men have been charged in connection with the hazing death of Trevor Duffy, a student at the University at Albany (UAlbany) who died in 2014 after being forced to drink a large amount of vodka as part of a fraternity initiation ritual.

**The Quest for Advanced Alien Civilizations**

A recent paper by astrophysicist Dan Hooper has revived an old idea from Russian astronomer Nikolai Kardashev's 1962 proposal to measure the level of technological advancement in civilizations across the universe. According to this model, there are three levels:

*   **Level I**: A civilization that can harness and use its planet's resources.
*   **Level II**: One that can capture energy directly from its star.

Hooper suggests that advanced alien civilizations may be detectable through their waste heat signatures or even visible as they harvest stars at incredible distances. This is because these aliens would need enormous amounts of power to sustain themselves millions of years before humanity. They could create swarms of satellites around their suns to collect solar radiation. Theorists have also explored megastructures like Dyson spheres.

In addition to searching for signs of harvesting stars, astronomers might look out for galaxies with missing prime mass due to being harvested by extraterrestrial beings. These hypothetical structures were first proposed by science fiction author Olaf Stapledon in his novel "Star Maker" published in 1937. Physicist Freeman Dyson later suggested similar concepts in a scientific paper in 1960. Astrophysicist Nikolai Kardashev further developed the concept in 1962, proposing that very old and advanced civilizations would fall into three categories based on their ability to harness energy:

1.  Type I: Harnessing planetary resources (e.g., Earth)
2.  Type II: Capturing stellar energy directly
3.  Type III: Harvesting galactic-scale energy sources

To achieve Level III status, a civilization would require immense energy reserves, which could potentially be harnessed using massive structures such as Dyson spheres. These mega-structures would involve billions of small spacecraft orbiting a star, collecting and concentrating its energy output.

While humans currently rate only 0.7 on the Kardashev scale, some scientists believe that more advanced civilizations thousands or even millions of years older than ours may already exist and be capable of constructing such mega-projects.

By monitoring the light emitted by distant stars and galaxies, astronomers hope to identify potential signs of advanced alien life forms engaged in large-scale energy collection activities. If successful, this approach could provide evidence of intelligent extraterrestrial life beyond our galaxy.

details.ground_truth: Watch out for stars moving across galaxies or losing power—it could be aliens gathering energy before the lights go out. Dan Hooper, an astronomy and astrophysics professor at the University of Chicago, posted a paper in the preprint journal arXiv.org arguing that aliens in far-off galaxies may be sucking energy from stars to offset risks posed by an expanding universe, LiveScience reports. "The presence of dark energy in our universe is causing space to expand at an accelerating rate," writes Hooper. "As a result, over the next approximately 100 billion years, all stars residing beyond the Local Group [of galaxies including the Milky Way] will fall beyond the cosmic horizon and become not only unobservable, but entirely inaccessible, thus limiting how much energy could one day be extracted from them." Therefore, he argues, an advanced civilization may use something like "Dyson spheres"—an imagined solar-powered satellite dating back to 1930s science-fiction, notes LiveScience—to harvest a star's energy or use that energy to move it closer to home. Hooper hinges his case on the work of Russian astronomer Nikolai Kardashev, who argued in 1962 that technologically advanced civilizations would expand via three steps: harvesting resources of their planet, then the nearest star, then all stars in the galaxy and nearby galaxies. So how to spot energy-grabbing aliens? Massive stars emanate certain light wavelengths, which will appear in galaxies' light signatures if stars are drained energy—that is, when humans have powerful enough instruments to detect it.

A 22-year-old employee was arrested on suspicion of detonating a dry ice bomb in Mickey's Toontown area of Disneyland, causing an explosion that briefly evacuated the section and sparked chaos among visitors.

Christian Barnes, who worked as an outdoor vendor for the resort, is being held on $1 million bail after detectives found fragments of a water bottle near the blast site and believe he placed dry ice inside it to create the explosion.

The incident occurred around 5:30 p.m. Tuesday evening when a plastic bottle containing dry ice exploded in a trash can, forcing officials to evacuate people from the area for two hours. No injuries were reported, but the explosion caused brief panic among young children visiting the popular theme park attraction.

Barnes has been cooperating with investigators and claims this was an isolated incident with unanticipated impacts. Police do not have a motive for the incident and say it does not appear connected to similar dry-ice explosions in Anaheim in recent months.

Disneyland released a statement saying they are working closely with authorities to investigate the matter. "We take matters like this very seriously," said Disney spokeswoman Suzi Brown.

Visitors expressed shock and concern over the incident, highlighting the need for safety precautions even in seemingly safe environments like amusement parks. The investigation into the incident continues.

The ensuing blast caused a lot of noise and chaos, but no injuries or serious damage, reports AP. No word on motive, but police don't think it's related to previous dry-ice bombs in the Anaheim area.

**Infant Battles Serious Infections and Health Issues**

A young infant named Oakleigh Ryan Nance has been fighting for her life due to multiple serious health issues. Born prematurely at 3 pounds, Oakleigh was initially considered a blessing after overcoming several challenges in the NICU (Neonatal Intensive Care Unit). However, she recently contracted two separate bacterial infections that have put her life at risk.

The first infection is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, an antibiotic-resistant bacteria commonly found in hospitals. This strain can cause severe symptoms, including sepsis, which can be deadly if left untreated. According to medical experts, people with weakened immune systems are more susceptible to this type of infection. Oakleigh's family is concerned about the severity of the infection, as it has already led to kidney reflux and heart problems.

In another alarming turn of events, Oakleigh also tested positive for E. coli, a "super strain" that doctors say could lead to brain damage or even death if not treated promptly. The source of the infection remains unknown, but investigators from the CDC are looking into the case. Due to Oakleigh's previous exposure to antibiotics, her family fears they may run out of treatment options soon.

To combat these health issues, Oakleigh is scheduled to undergo surgery on August 10th to address her stage 3 kidney reflux. Her family is trying to raise funds through GoFundMe to cover the associated medical expenses. Despite the dire situation, Oakleigh's loved ones remain hopeful, citing their faith in God as a source of strength during this challenging time.

As Oakleigh continues to battle against overwhelming odds, her story serves as a reminder of the importance of healthcare awareness and support for families facing similar struggles.
details.ground_truth: An Oklahoma girl diagnosed with "super" E. coli is facing a life-or-death battle—and worse, she's only 11 months old. "With this strain of E. coli, it can get in her brain, it can get in her spinal cord, basically cause her to go into cardiac arrest," her grandfather, Chris Curtis, tells KFOR. "And we heard that it was a very, very scary situation." Her family says it's not clear how Oakleigh Nance got the infection, which appears resistant to antibiotics, but the CDC is investigating. It all started when Oakleigh was born premature at only 3 pounds and "started off on 4 liters of oxygen," according to a GoFundMe page to help pay her medical bills. "In the NICU, they used to call her Miss Sassy because of her ability to express her displeasure with her circumstances," the page says. Then she went home and was fine for months until a 104-degree temperature and severe urinary tract infection sent her back to the hospital. Since then, she's been diagnosed with moderate ASD and pulmonary stenosis of the heart, stage 3 kidney reflux, and "a dangerous, antibiotic resistant strain of Pseudomonas," says the GoFundMe page. Now doctors are planning a 4 1/2-hour procedure on her kidney, which is functioning at 22%, to possibly prevent other infections. "I know that God is in control of all else, and when I think about what’s going on in her life, I think about my faith in God," says Curtis. "That’s what sustains me and gets me through it." **Portland Water Crisis: 38 Million Gallons Flushed After Urine Incident**

A bizarre incident at Portland's Mt. Tabor Reservoir has led to the flushing of 38 million gallons of drinking water after an 18-year-old man was caught on surveillance video urinating in the reservoir early Wednesday morning. The individual, later identified as Dallas Swonger, claims he did not pee into the water supply but rather onto a wall next to it.

According to reports, Swonger and two friends were seen trespassing at Mount Tabor Park around 1 am when they decided to skateboard and hang out near the uncovered reservoirs. During this time, Swonger allegedly relieved himself against a nearby wall while his friend Trey McDaniel claimed that animals often die in the reservoir due to various reasons including urine contamination.

However, city officials insist that Swonger indeed peed into the water supply, prompting them to flush 38 million gallons of clean drinking water down the drain despite test results showing no signs of toxins or contaminants from human waste. This decision drew criticism from experts who pointed out that the risk of health hazards is extremely low given the dilution factor of such large quantities of water.

The move also sparked debate among residents with some questioning whether politics played a role in the decision-making process. City Commissioner Nick Fish defended the decision stating that any potential risks outweighed by the need for public trust in their ability to provide safe drinking water.

Swonger granted an exclusive interview to Vocativ where he denied intentionally contaminating the water supply and expressed frustration over being portrayed as reckless and irresponsible. He stated that he had just moved back to town and wanted to spend quality time with friends before graduating high school.

As investigations continue, Swonger faces additional charges related to trespassing and public urination. His mother apologized publicly saying her son "is trying to get his life together" following graduation.

In conclusion, the controversy surrounding the flushing of millions of gallons of clean drinking water highlights concerns about public policy decisions made under pressure and raises questions regarding the effectiveness of measures taken to protect public safety.

Possible criminal charges are still pending, the Oregonian notes. The paper also reports that the water tested clean of urine-related toxins, but all 38 million gallons will still be dumped.

**911 Dispatcher's Quick Thinking Saves Woman Trapped in Car Trunk**

On January 14th, a Johnston County emergency dispatcher named Tim Medlin played a crucial role in saving a woman who was trapped in the trunk of her boyfriend's car. The incident occurred around 4am when the 29-year-old woman called 911 to report that she had been locked inside the trunk by her jealous boyfriend.

Medlin, a shift supervisor at the time, quickly sprang into action despite being unable to understand much of what the caller said due to poor phone reception and background noise. He used an old flip phone provided for landline notifications to text the woman instead of calling back on his regular line. To everyone's surprise, the woman responded with vital information about their location - a red Mustang traveling down I-95 towards Fayetteville.

With this new lead, dispatchers were able to track the vehicle using cell phone tracking technology and alert local authorities. Police officers from the Fayetteville department apprehended Nicholas Mattevi (32) near the city limits and charged him with false imprisonment. Fortunately, the woman was found unharmed after being rescued from the trunk.

The quick thinking and resourcefulness displayed by Medlin have sparked calls for updating 911 centers' communication systems to allow them to initiate texts directly rather than relying on receiving messages only. Jason Barbour, director of the Johnston County Emergency Communications Center, praised Medlin's actions as "a prime example of technology being used to its fullest potential" during times of crisis.

Mattevi has since posted bail and is awaiting trial. This harrowing ordeal serves as a testament to the importance of effective emergency response systems and the bravery of individuals like Tim Medlin who put themselves forward to save others in need.
details.ground_truth: A North Carolina woman allegedly locked in the trunk of a moving car by her boyfriend was saved by a quick-thinking 911 dispatcher and a lowly flip phone, ABC News reports. The 29-year-old woman called 911 around 4am Jan. 14. The woman had gotten in a fight with her boyfriend, who was "jealous," according to WRAL. Before dispatcher Tim Medlin could get much information from the woman, the call was dropped. He was unable to get her to answer when he called back. Then Medlin remembered a flip phone the 911 communications center keeps around in case the phone lines go down, WTVD reports. He says texting was the only way he could think to contact her without getting "her in trouble." The woman texted Medlin back, letting the dispatcher know she was in a red Mustang headed toward Fayetteville. Verizon provided the location of the woman's phone, and police stopped her and her boyfriend, Nicholas Mattevi, in Fayetteville. Mattevi, 32, was arrested and charged with false imprisonment. "I can go to bed," Medlin recalls feeling upon hearing of the arrest. "We've done our job." He says he's planning to buy a smartphone for the office to replace the old flip phone and make it easier to text if there's a next time. Medlin's boss tells ABC the dispatcher "really stood by our motto: Failure is not an option." (This 911 dispatcher was accused of hanging up on callers.)

**Ancient Human Innovations Challenge Traditional Views on Modern Humanity**

Recent discoveries in Kenya's Olorgesailie Basin have shed new light on human evolution and behavior. Excavations by an international team of scientists reveal that early humans were more advanced than previously thought.

The oldest stone tools found at the site date back to 320,000 years ago, tens of thousands earlier than initially believed. The researchers propose that climate change may have driven these innovations, as well as other technological advancements such as obsidian blades and pigment production. These findings suggest that modern behaviors emerged much earlier than expected, challenging traditional views on human revolution.

According to paleoanthropologist Rick Potts, "I think it is clear now that our ancestors' ability to adapt was far greater than we had imagined." 

These studies also show evidence for complex social networks, with people trading goods over long distances. This suggests that hominin populations interacted extensively before Homo sapiens emergence. In fact, Brooks says, this period saw significant cultural exchange between groups.

In addition, archaeologists Alison Lahr notes that Middle Stone Age technology remained relatively unchanged from 300,000-500,000 years ago. However, there are signs of gradual changes in tool-making techniques during this time frame. It remains unclear how exactly these developments relate to different species coexisting across Africa.

Overall, recent research has significantly expanded understanding of ancient humanity, revealing sophisticated societies existed hundreds of thousands of years prior to what was once considered the dawn of modernity.
details.ground_truth: For decades, the human story was one told through signs of modernity—art, tools, burials—found only after Homo sapiens left Africa. Recent discoveries pushing back the date of departure are helping to change that narrative, as are three new studies in Science. Together, they describe the earliest stone tools of their kind in East Africa as well as the earliest evidence for long-distance transport of raw materials in the region, per Science News. Researchers previously believed the Early Stone Age marked by large, primitive tools (hand axes and cleavers) made way for the Middle Stone Age and its smaller tools (spearpoints and blades) around 280,000 years ago. But stone tools found in Kenya's Olorgesailie Basin show hominin groups—it's not clear which species is responsible—had developed these more advanced tools approximately 320,000 years ago. "We see a smaller technology, a more diverse series of stone tools … designed for specific purposes," researcher Rick Potts tells NPR. An expert not involved in the study says the tools are so "prepared and retouched" they suggest the Middle Stone Age likely started even earlier. What drove it? Microscopic and chemical analyses of the region's soil show the landscape was rapidly shifting between wet and dry conditions, meaning hominins might have been forced to adapt. But as the technology also coincides with the emergence of Homo sapiens in Africa, it's possible that the human mind deserves credit. The tools themselves suggest the development of trading networks, too. Some were made of rocks carried from 55 miles away, says Potts. Others were made of obsidian from as far as 30 miles away, per the Conversation. (These stone tools are also making waves.)

In response to the recent mass shooting at an Oregon community college that left nine people dead, Donald Trump has made several comments on gun control and mass shootings.

"If you had some very good guys with guns inside that room," he said, "it would've been over." 

Trump also mentioned having a handgun carry permit in New York State and claimed that mental illness is the root cause of such tragedies. In an interview with NBC's Meet the Press, he acknowledged that there will always be problems but emphasized self-defense as a solution. When asked about stricter regulations, he replied, "I don't think so."

At another rally in Nashville, Trump referenced Charles Bronson from Death Wish (1974) saying he'd emulate him if someone attacked him. The crowd responded enthusiastically when he shouted out the movie title together. This was not the first time Trump linked himself to this film; during a previous event, he used it to illustrate his stance on gun ownership.

The Republican frontrunner argued against increased firearms regulation after the Umpqua Community College massacre, suggesting instead that more emphasis should be placed on addressing mental health issues. His views are seen as shifting since launching his campaign six months ago, where previously he advocated for stronger controls.

He told a rally in Nashville on Saturday that "it's not the guns, it's the people. It's these sick people," the AP reports. "Many states and many cities are closing their mental health facilities and closing them down, and they're closing them because they don't have the funding. And we have to start looking much stronger into mental health," he said. On NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday, Trump explained that gun control wouldn't help because "they can be sick as hell and they’re geniuses in a certain way.
