He brought up Charles Bronson's Death Wish, got the audience to chant the name of the movie, and said: "Today you can’t make that movie because it’s not politically correct," reports the Guardian. (Jeb Bush took a lot of heat for saying "Stuff happens" after the Oregon shooting.)

**Apple's iPhone 7 and AirPods Controversy**

At Apple's recent product launch event, marketing chief Phil Schiller announced that the new iPhone 7 would no longer have a standard headphone jack, instead opting for wireless audio with its proprietary Lightning connector or through Bluetooth connectivity using the new AirPods.

The decision has been met with widespread criticism from tech enthusiasts and critics alike, who argue that this move is unnecessary and will inconvenience users. Many pointed out that there was no technological reason to remove the headphone jack, as it had become an industry standard.

Schiller attempted to justify the decision by saying that it required "courage," but his words were quickly mocked on social media. Critics argued that courage involves taking risks in the face of adversity, not removing features that people rely on without providing adequate alternatives.

Several writers, including Chris Taylor (@FutureBoy) and Richard Hay (@WinObs), expressed their disappointment and frustration with the decision, pointing out that it will force users to buy expensive adapters or switch to wireless headphones like the $159 AirPods. They also noted that the removal of the headphone jack is not comparable to previous design changes made by Apple, such as eliminating the CD drive or floppy disk slot.

One writer joked about how Apple's mantra of "it just works" is now officially dead, citing the complexity and potential hassle of dealing with wireless headphones and adapters. Another compared the situation to San Francisco's gentrification policies, where low-income residents are being priced out of their own city – implying that Apple is similarly pricing out consumers who can't afford the latest technology.

Overall, the reaction to Apple's decision to eliminate the headphone jack has been overwhelmingly negative, with many calling it a step backward for innovation and user experience. As one critic put it, "Courage is buying $159 Air Pods and then going home to tell your spouse what you bought."
details.ground_truth: Apple presented its new smartphone Wednesday, and nestled in with the iPhone 7's much-ballyhooed features was the disclosure that the company is getting rid of the phone's headphone jack—news that wasn't exactly met with universal acclaim, or much acclaim at all. Chris Taylor is one detractor of the headphone ditch, writing for Mashable that, in nearly 20 years of attending Apple product launches, he's "never heard anything as ridiculous emanate from that stage as I did Wednesday." Apple marketing head Phil Schiller used the word "courage" to describe Apple's innovation, but that's not how Taylor sees it. "Courage is marching across the Edmund Pettus bridge in Selma in 1965 [or] facing down a tank in Tiananmen Square," he writes. "Courage, by definition, involves doing something that makes you afraid." Apparently Taylor doesn't think Apple was quivering in its workboots when it came up with this plan. He's got plenty of other words instead of "courage" in mind, including "hubris," "arrogance," "greed," and his personal favorite, "stupidity," which he attributes to Apple for taking "one step forward, two steps back" both technologically ("wired almost always sounds better than wireless") and logistically (no more plugging in other peripherals like credit card readers, for example). Meanwhile, although much of the other feedback online is similarly cranky about the headphone jack's demise, Quartz notes that Apple is actually late, not early, in making this move: A handful of Chinese smartphone brands have been fiddling around with the idea for years, and some have already sent these phones, sans jacks, to market.

**A Teacher's Unwavering Love and Support Lead to Adoption**

In 1981, Linda Hooper met her student Cruz Riojas, who would later become her son through an adoption process in 1998. At first, Mrs. Hooper described Cruz as "a holy terror" due to his violent outbursts and behavior in class. However, she refused to give up on him.

Over time, Cruz began to change, and he eventually became part of their family. He was adopted by the Hoopers when he turned 18 years old, but it wasn't until after graduating from Texas Tech University that they formally adopted him in 1998.

Today, Cruz is married with two children and works as payroll manager for Corporate Solutions in San Antonio. The Hoopers are proud grandparents to Hannah (13) and Greyson (9). They live together in San Antonio.

The story highlights the impact one person can make in someone else's life. Despite initial reservations, Linda Hooper took Cruz under her wing and provided love and support throughout his difficult teenage years. Her unwavering dedication ultimately led to Cruz becoming a permanent member of their family.

Linda Hooper said that adopting Cruz was not just about providing a loving home; it was also about recognizing the incredible potential within him. She believes that every child deserves a chance to succeed, regardless of their background or circumstances.

This remarkable true story serves as a testament to the transformative power of kindness, compassion, and determination. It shows us that even in the face of adversity, there is always hope for redemption and new beginnings.

details.ground_truth: An operation in London has given 9-year-old Kieran Sorkin a pair of ears—made from his ribs, no less. "I'd like just to look like my friends. I'd also like to be able to wear sunglasses and earphones." So surgeons traced an outline of Kieran's mom's ears, removed cartilage from the boy's ribs, and sliced, contoured, and sewed the cartilage. Then they put it in two skin pockets and vacuumed them into the shape of ears. They don't perform any function, but Kieran's plastic surgeon says they can deliver a huge confidence boost: "If you can change the confidence of a patient at this young age, you can change their whole trajectory in life," he said. The ears should last, too, because they're made of cartilage rather than prosthetics, the Guardian reports. Every year about 100 British newborns lack one or both ears (it's called microtia), and the hospital Kieran went to performs the operation about 40 times a year. Scientists hope to one day make ears from the fat tissue of patients, instead of ribs. Kieran might have liked that, since he got so excited on seeing his new ears that he cried "Wow!" and giggled—which made his ribs hurt from the operation. **Wild Panda Attack Compensation**

A Chinese villager has been awarded over $83,000 in compensation after being attacked by a wild panda on his farmland last year.

Guan Quanzhi, 52, was working on his land in Li Baizi village, Gansu province when a wild panda chased by other villagers ran onto his property and bit him severely on the leg. The incident occurred on March 1, 2014, leaving Guan with serious injuries that required eight surgeries to repair.

The attack highlights the dangers posed by wild pandas, which are often perceived as harmless due to their lovable appearance. However, they are members of the bear family and have powerful jaws capable of inflicting severe bites.

Despite conservation efforts, wild pandas remain under pressure from habitat loss and low reproductive rates. According to official data cited by state media, the number of wild giant pandas rose nearly 17% between 2003 and 2013 to reach 1,864, thanks to conservation measures.

In this case, local forestry officials and the management bureau of Baishuijiang Natural Reserve agreed to pay Guan 520,000 yuan ($83,000) in compensation for his medical expenses and potential future operations. Guan's son had initially sued three government departments responsible for controlling wild animals, leading to negotiations that resulted in the settlement.

This is not an isolated incident; there have been previous cases where humans were injured or killed by wild pandas. In 2008, a 20-year-old man was mauled by a panda at a zoo in southern China.

Pandas are also a major tourist draw in several parts of China, generating significant revenue through rentals to foreign zoos. Despite these economic benefits, the risks associated with interacting with wild pandas should not be underestimated.

As WWF notes on its website, "a panda can protect itself as well as most other bears" using its heavy weight, strong jaw muscles, and large molar teeth. While attacks are rare, it serves as a reminder of the importance of respecting wildlife boundaries and taking necessary precautions around wild animals.
details.ground_truth: Pandas may prefer their meals in the form of bamboo, but that doesn't mean their bite is toothless. **Jamaica Decriminalizes Possession of Small Amounts of Marijuana**

In a historic move, Jamaica's parliament has passed legislation decriminalizing possession of small amounts of marijuana, also known as "ganja", making it a petty offense with no criminal record attached to it. The law change is expected to pave way for the development of medical cannabis industry in the island nation.

The new law makes up to 2 ounces (56 grams) of ganja legal use and cultivation of industrial hemp, which can be used for various purposes such as textiles, food products, and other goods. This will create jobs and stimulate economic growth on the Caribbean island country.

This comes after years of debate over relaxing laws surrounding the drug that was made illegal decades ago. Previous attempts at reforming were met by opposition from Washington due to international pressure but now emboldened by changes in U.S states like Colorado, Alaska, and others have led to this breakthrough.

Tourists who are prescribed medicinal pot abroad may soon apply for permits to legally purchase weed while visiting the island. However, recreational use remains prohibited under Jamaican law.

Local scientists already produce Canasol eye drops using CBD oil extracted from marijuana plants. They hope to expand their product line into more therapeutic uses.

Commerce Minister Anthony Hylton said the cannabis industry holds great potential for Jamaica, where many people grow marijuana illegally. He added that the government plans to establish regulations for licensing authority and refining details of the medical sector.

"This is big step forward," Delano Seiveright, director of Cannabis Commercial Taskforce, stated. "But there still much work ahead."

International trend shows easing restrictions on marijuana across Americas. More than 20 US states allow some form of marijuana legalization or decriminalization. Uruguay became first country worldwide last year legalize sale of marijuana nationwide.

Note: I condensed Passage 1 & 3 together since they contain similar information about the passage of the bill in Jamaica.
details.ground_truth: Alaska yesterday became the third state to legalize marijuana for recreational use, and now a country where you would have thought that was the case already is moving closer to that goal itself. Jamaica's parliament last night approved a law decriminalizing small amounts of pot, the AP reports. People found with 2 ounces or less of marijuana will now simply receive a ticket—not a crime on their record—and cultivation of five plants or fewer is now allowed. A licensing agency was also established to oversee pot cultivation and distribution for medical and scientific efforts. Rastafarians are rejoicing, because the bill also grants them the legal right to use cannabis for sacramental purposes, while tourists who have medical marijuana prescriptions elsewhere can pay for permits to buy a bit of ganja on the island. Jamaica has shied away from decriminalization because it didn't want to risk violating international treaties and provoking US sanctions, the Guardian reports. The process for the new law was described by National Security Minister Peter Bunting as an "elephantine," nearly 40-year effort, ABC Australia reports. "[The law] eliminates an unnecessary source of friction between police and citizens, and ensures that our young people are not gratuitously shackled with criminal records," he said in a statement. Jamaica also hopes to boost its health tourism and medical marijuana industries and make it a major player in the pot product market, the Guardian notes. International exporting, however, remains a no-no. A US counternarcotics official told the AP in an email that "Jamaican law is of course Jamaica's own business," but warned that drug trafficking into the US is still illegal.

On December 28, AirAsia's Airbus A320-200 plane carrying 162 people from Indonesia to Singapore crashed into the Java Sea, killing everyone on board.

Search teams have found four large parts of the aircraft wreckage on the seafloor, including an engine and two wings. The breakthrough came after nearly a week-long search operation in choppy waters. Indonesian officials said they are confident that many more bodies will be retrieved soon.

AirAsia CEO Tony Fernandes expressed his condolences to the families affected and promised a thorough investigation into the incident. The company is also reviewing its suspension of flights between Surabaya and Singapore.

"Flight 8501 appears to have been trapped in bad weather that would have been difficult to avoid," says a report by Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency.

**Habeas Corpus and Animal Rights: A Double-Edged Sword**

The concept of habeas corpus has been at the forefront of two significant cases in recent times. This ancient legal procedure allows individuals to challenge their detention or imprisonment by demanding that authorities show cause for it.

In the first case, the Military Commissions Act (MCA) of 2006 effectively suspended habeas corpus rights for non-citizens detained at Guantanamo Bay. The US government's treatment of detainees there has raised concerns about human rights abuses and indefinite detention without trial. Despite several court victories, including a Supreme Court ruling in June 2013, many Guantánamo detainees remain imprisoned with little hope of release.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the law, animal rights activists have taken up the mantle of habeas corpus as well. In New York State, a judge granted a writ of habeas corpus to two research chimpanzees, Hercules and Leo, who are being held captive at Stony Brook University. If successful, this would be the first time in U.S history that animals were recognized as persons under the law." 

However, not everyone is convinced that these developments will lead to major breakthroughs. Richard Cupp, a law professor at Pepperdine University, believes that today’s decision should not be seen as a victory for NhRP just yet. He argues that the judge may simply need more information before making a final decision.

Despite these differing opinions, Natalie Prosin, executive director of Nonhuman Rights Project, sees today's development as an important step forward. She notes that even if they lose the case, the group can use the habeas corpus ruling to sway judges in other jurisdictions.

Ultimately, both cases highlight the complexities surrounding habeas corpus and its application beyond traditional human subjects. As we continue to grapple with issues related to national security, individual liberties, and animal welfare, these decisions serve as reminders of the ongoing struggle between power and justice.
details.ground_truth: The writ of habeas corpus lets prisoners appear in court to make their captors justify why they're being held. Until now in the US, those who've used this legal tactic have been human. But a New York judge yesterday ruled that the writ may be used by two lab chimpanzees at Stony Brook University, Science magazine reports. NY Supreme Court Justice Barbara Jaffe ordered a university rep to address a suit filed by the Nonhuman Rights Project by appearing in court May 6 to argue why the college is holding Hercules and Leo. The group, which says the animals are being detained for biomedical experiments, says its ultimate goal is to have the animals released to the Save the Chimps sanctuary in Fort Pierce, Fla., per the NhRP's website. "This is a big step forward to getting what we are ultimately seeking: the right to bodily liberty for chimpanzees and other cognitively complex animals," Natalie Prosin, the project's executive director, tells Science. The case kicked off in December 2013 with lawsuits that also included two chimps held on private property; each case was struck down, sending the NhRP down the appeals path. Not everyone's convinced the upcoming hearing will mean liberation for the chimps. A Pepperdine University law professor tells Science that the judge likely just wants to hear both sides of the story: "It would be quite surprising if the judge intended to make a momentous substantive finding that chimpanzees are legal persons" without doing so, he notes. Prosin, meanwhile, says her group isn't stopping with the chimps and will also target the release of other animals. (Click to read about what chimps talk to each other about.)

**Gibson Guitar Raid and Lacey Act Controversy**

In September 2011, federal marshals raided Gibson Guitar Corporation's facilities in Tennessee for allegedly trafficking in illegally sourced wood from Madagascar. This is not the first time the company has been targeted by authorities; a similar raid occurred in November 2009.

The government appears to be preparing charges against Gibson under the Lacey Act, a century-old endangered species law that was amended in 2008 to include environmental regulations. The act prohibits the importation or sale of goods made with materials obtained through illegal means.

According to court documents, Gibson imported ebony from Madagascar without proper documentation, which may have violated the Lacey Act. However, the company claims it complied with all relevant laws and regulations at the time.

Andrea Johnson, director of forest programs at the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), says that Gibson knowingly imported contraband wood despite being aware of its illegality. She argues that the Lacey Act requires end-users like Gibson to verify the origin of their wood imports.

Other guitar manufacturers are also affected by the controversy surrounding the Lacey Act. Chris Martin, CEO of C.F. Martin & Company, warns that the law can lead to unintended consequences, such as requiring companies to prove the provenance of vintage instruments.

**Rabies Outbreak in Maine**

A recent outbreak of rabies has left several residents shaken and on high alert for potential threats from infected animals.

According to reports, 21-year-old Rachel Borch was attacked by a rabid raccoon while jogging near her home in Hope, Maine on June 3rd. The animal latched onto her thumb before she managed to drown it in a puddle using only her bare hands. Fortunately, the raccoon later tested positive for rabies at the state's Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

This incident is not an isolated case; earlier this week, a Wiscasset man was bitten by a suspected rabid fox in Topsham. As of June 7th, there have been **20 confirmed cases of rabies in animals across Maine**, with many more potentially affected areas under investigation.

Maine CDC data shows that last year saw **64 reported cases of rabies in animals**, highlighting the growing concern among local authorities. According to Heidi Blood, Animal Control Officer in Hope, "If you see something acting strangely or erratically, don't approach it."

Rachel Borch received six shots as part of her treatment after being exposed to the virus through the bite wound. She will receive her final shot over the weekend. Her harrowing experience serves as a stark reminder of the importance of taking precautions when interacting with wildlife.

Residents are advised to remain vigilant and report any suspicious behavior around wild animals. While attacks like these can be traumatic, prompt medical attention and proper vaccination protocols significantly reduce the risk of contracting rabies.

In light of these incidents, public awareness campaigns aim to educate people about the risks associated with rabies-infected animals and encourage responsible pet ownership practices. By staying informed and proactive, we can work together to minimize the threat posed by this deadly disease.

Yanking out her headphones, she began "dancing" around the animal on the narrow path, but she tells the Herald she knew that, one way or another, the animal was going to bite her. She figured her hands would be the best spot, so she offered them up. The raccoon chomped down on her thumb and stayed there, scratching at her legs and arms as she screamed. Now on her knees, she spotted her phone lying submerged in a mud puddle, and had an idea: drown it. "With my thumb in its mouth, I just pushed its head down into the muck," she tells the News. When the raccoon finally stopped moving, she yanked out her finger and raced the three-quarters of a mile home. Two days later, the state confirmed the animal was infected with rabies. Borch got rabies shots, and an animal control officer adds an unpleasant footnote: The infected raccoon may not be alone. "Not to scare people," Heidi Blood tells the News, but "when there’s one, there’s typically another." (Normally nocturnal like raccoons, a crazed beaver attacked a woman paddle-boarder.)

**Ancient Mars Was Once Home to Massive Ocean and May Have Been Habitable**

New research from NASA scientists has revealed that ancient Mars was once home to an ocean covering nearly half its surface, making it a more promising place for alien life to exist. The findings are based on measurements taken over six years using some of the world's most powerful telescopes.

The study found that four billion years ago, there existed at least 137 meters deep global ocean which would have been enough if it covered the entire planet evenly. However, given Martian terrain today, they believe it likely only reached about 20% of the northern hemisphere. This massive body of water lasted millions of years before thinning atmosphere led to loss in space. Today, just 13% remains locked up as ice caps.

Astronomers also discovered evidence suggesting that early Mars had identical proportions of ordinary hydrogen (H) and deuterium (D), similar to Earth. But due to weaker gravity allowing H escape into outer space, this ratio changed significantly over time. As a result, modern-day Mars' atmospheric vapor contains seven times higher levels of D than EARTH does.

These results add new insights into what made young Mars habitable. Scientists now think that with such large amounts of liquid water present, conditions were ripe for microbial life forms like those seen elsewhere in our solar system. While no conclusive proof exists yet, ongoing missions will continue searching for signs of past or current biological activity on the Red Planet.

NASA plans further exploration through their Exomars rover mission set to launch next year; meanwhile Curiosity continues studying methane emissions detected last year sparking speculation regarding potential biosignatures.
details.ground_truth: Imagine all the water in the Arctic Ocean. Now, imagine all that and more on Mars. If you visited the Red Planet roughly 4.3 billion years ago, that's what you likely would have found, say NASA scientists. Their new study arrived at that "solid estimate ... by determining how much water was lost to space," says lead author Geronimo Villanueva. The Guardian reports the scientists used three powerful infrared telescopes to analyze two forms of water in Mars' atmosphere: H2O and HDO, in which deuterium (aka "heavy" hydrogen) has taken the place of one hydrogen atom. As National Geographic explains, Mars' gravity is weaker than our own; that allowed hydrogen to escape from the atmosphere and into space over time, boosting the amount of deuterium in its water. Scientists compared the ratio of HDO to H2O in Martian water today with that in water from a 4.5 billion-year-old Mars meteorite to arrive at their conclusions, a press release states. They ultimately calculated that Mars was once home to 20 million cubic kilometers of ocean. It could have covered every inch of the planet in water 450 feet deep, but the scientists think a different scenario is more likely: that the ocean covered roughly a fifth of the planet, was located in the northern hemisphere, and was as much as a mile deep. While National Geographic observes the findings back up "reams of earlier evidence that water once existed on the surface" of Mars, another study author points out the assessment of the degree of water lost indicates something new. "The planet was very likely wet for a longer period of time than was previously thought, suggesting it might have been habitable for longer," a scientist says. (Mysterious plumes on Mars are stumping scientists.)

**University Professor Helps Rescue Student and Family from ISIS**

In 2014, Swedish chemistry professor Charlotta Turner received a desperate text message from her graduate student Firas Jumaah, who was hiding with his family in a disused bleach factory in Iraq due to the threat posed by ISIS warriors. Jumaah's wife had rung him to say that Isis fighters had taken over their next-door village, killing men and taking women into slavery.

Turner, determined not to leave her student to die without trying to do something, contacted the university's security chief Per Gustafson, who arranged for a rescue operation through a private security company. Over several days, two Landcruisers carrying heavily-armed mercenaries were sent to extract Jumaah and his family from the war zone.

The situation was dire as ISIS forces advanced on their location, coming within just 12 miles of their house. Despite this danger, Turner remained committed to helping her student and approached the university's security team to find a solution. The rescue mission ultimately succeeded, and Jumaah and his family were safely evacuated to Erbil Airport before being reunited with Turner back in Sweden.

Jumaah has since completed his PhD at Lund University and now works for a pharmaceuticals company in Malmö. His family is still paying off the debt incurred during the rescue operation, which was facilitated by the university. This extraordinary event highlights the lengths to which some individuals will go to help those in need, even when faced with seemingly insurmountable challenges.

Gustafson noted that no other university has been involved in such an extensive rescue effort, underscoring the unique circumstances surrounding Jumaah's case. For Turner, it was simply a matter of doing what she could to save someone under her care. "It was obvious that I should help," she said, reflecting on the experience.
details.ground_truth: Four years ago, a chemistry professor got a text from her grad student: If I'm not back in a week, cut me from the doctoral program. Charlotta Turner called him right away: "He was very sad and crying,” the 48-year-old prof at Lund University in Sweden tells NBC News. "I could hear that the situation was hopeless and they had to flee." The student, Firas Jumaah, was visiting his native Iraq to help family members during a brutal 2014 ISIS attack targeting Yazidis—a religious minority that includes his family. The terror group had just enslaved and massacred Yazidis by the thousand in nearby Sinjar. Now Jumaah and family were planning to flee to the mountains. "I had no hope at all," says Jumaah, per the Local. "I was desperate." But Turner took action. She spoke to Lund University's then-security chief, who contacted a company that sent mercenaries into northern Iraq. Only days later, four armed mercs on two Landcruisers blazed into the place where Jumaah was hiding, and rushed him to Erbil Airport with his wife and two young kids. "I have never felt so privileged, so VIP," he says. "But at the same time I felt like a coward as I left my mother and sisters behind me." Seeing his colleagues back in Sweden, he was speechless: "I just cried," he says. Yet Jumaah finished his PhD and found work at a Malmo pharmaceuticals company, and his family survived. The bill: roughly 60,000 kroner ($6,613), which his family has nearly finished paying. “If they told me to pay 200,000 kronor, I would,” says Jumaah. (The UN is finding fresh ISIS horrors.)

The film follows Nicky's partnership with Jess Barrett (Margot Robbie), a young woman who learns the art of deception from him.

According to critics, the movie is more about showcasing Will Smith's jaded charm than delivering an authentic story. Despite its absurd plot twists and ridiculous details, the film manages to entertain thanks to Smith's charisma and Margot Robbie's convincing performance as the femme fatale.

In fact, the casting process for Focus was quite dramatic in itself, with several A-list actors being considered for the lead roles before settling on Will Smith and Margot Robbie. Ryan Gosling, Brad Pitt, Ben Affleck, Jennifer Lawrence, Emma Stone, and many others were reportedly approached at some point during the production.

Will Smith's character suits him perfectly, given his ability to convincingly play charming characters throughout his career. From his early days as a rapper to his breakout role in "The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air," Smith has consistently demonstrated his talent for playing smooth-talking individuals who effortlessly navigate high society.

While Focus may not be a particularly original or well-written script, it does have moments of genuine humor and wit, courtesy of Adrian Martinez's comedic relief and BD Wong's memorable turn as a shady businessman. Overall, the film approaches modest goals and delivers an entertaining experience, largely due to the chemistry between its leads and their undeniable star power.

details.ground_truth: Will Smith stars as Nicky, an established con man who takes on a new apprentice, Australian newcomer Margot Robbie's Jess, in Focus. They both love the con game, but who's playing who? Here's what critics are saying: Richard Corliss at Time is a fan. "The mix of longtime star and minx on the rise is one tasty element in the success of a movie that approaches the modest goals and effortless allure of a 60-year-old Hitchcock," he writes. Smith "takes a welcome break from glowering sci-fi roles" and writer-directors Glenn Ficarra and John Requa "deserve some credit in letting Will be Will in the star's first charm barrage since 2005's Hitch." Steven Rea at the Philadelphia Inquirer admits Smith "shows some of the movie-star wattage that's been missing from his recent pics. He charms." There's also "combustible chemistry" between Smith and Robbie, but the movie just "disappoints," Rea writes. "Even if you're willing to forgive its sinkhole plotholes and farthest-fetched conceits, the film ... ultimately makes no sense." Betsy Sharkey, on the other hand, says this "rom-com-con" is "an irresistible reminder of all the reasons we first fell for the Fresh Prince so many years ago." Writing at the Los Angeles Times, she notes the romantic role of Nicky fits Smith perfectly, while Robbie is "more than holding her own" as his match. "The scams are Rubik's Cube complicated, but what keeps you guessing is whether the romantic connection between Jess and Nicky is real or just another con." But Mick LaSalle at the San Francisco Chronicle isn't convinced. In a review titled "Will Smith just stole $12 from your pocket," he argues Focus is "ridiculous in every detail. It's a movie with no truth that teaches nothing and shows nothing, that has only its audacity to recommend it." Nicky and Jess lack "impact," partly because "Smith is not a strong leading man," he says. Viewers are left "waiting for the trick, which is not the same as being fooled."

A long-running legal battle between global chocolate giants Nestlé and Mondelez over the shape of KitKat finger wafers has been sent back to the European Union's trademark office after judges dismissed appeals by both companies.

The case began in 2002 when Nestle sought Europe-wide protection for its iconic four-finger wafer biscuit bars across the bloc. NEWLINE_CHAR The ruling means that EUIPO must review an earlier decision made in favor of Swiss-based company’s trademark on the shape. 

In this year, it was reported that Cadbury had lost a similar trademark dispute with Lindt chocolatier in Britain. In another instance, Toblerone owner Mondelz won a case against Poundland which designed a copycat version of their triangular-shaped bar.

Nestle believes that Wednesday's judgement is not the end of the road and will continue fighting for the trademark. However, experts say that the ruling could bring an end to the protected status of the Kit Kat shape within the EU.

This development comes as other countries have different rules regarding trademarks. For example, while the UK court ruled that the Kit Kat shape cannot be trademarked due to lack of distinctiveness, France still recognizes the trademark.

Experts believe that this ruling may set a precedent for future cases involving brand recognition and intellectual property rights.

It remains unclear what implications this ruling will have on brands operating across the EU single market. However, it is clear that the outcome of this case will have significant consequences for businesses relying on trademark protections.

details.ground_truth: "Four trapezoidal bars aligned on a rectangular base" may not be instantly recognizable. What that means, however, is that if the EU Intellectual Property Office finds, based on more recent evidence, that the KitKat bar's shape is recognizable in enough countries, it can retain the trademark protection, per Reuters. The brand name itself of "KitKat" is not being contested. (Atari accused Nestle of ripping off one of its popular video games in an ad for KitKat.)

details.ground_truth: Dinosaurs may have been much more like modern birds than we knew—and not just because some had feathers. A new study suggests that mighty dinosaurs of yore didn't roar, contrary to every dinosaur movie you've ever seen. Instead, they made a decidedly less scary sound called a "closed-mouth vocalization." Think of a dove cooing or perhaps an ostrich doing this grunting thing. As the scientists explain in the journal Evolution, per UT News, the sound actually comes out of the neck area after air is pushed through an esophageal pouch. In fact, the animal's mouth is shut the whole time. Lots of birds do this today, and because birds descended from dinosaurs, scientists suspect they may have communicated in a similar way. The fossil record can't prove it, though the Washington Post notes that previous research meshes with the idea, including the belief that dinosaurs had air sacs instead of vocal chords. “A cool thing about this work is the demonstration that closed-mouth behavior evolved many times,” says the lead author. “That suggests it can emerge fairly easily and be incorporated into mating displays" among different types of animals. A co-author says the study gives the impression of "a very different Jurassic world. Not only were dinosaurs feathered, but they may have had bulging necks and made booming, closed-mouth sounds." But if so, the makers of Jurassic Park didn't get it all wrong: The hiss of the film's velociraptors came from a goose, per Vulture. (Scientists have grown chickens with dinosaur legs.)

**Double Homicide in Fort Worth**

A shocking incident occurred on Sunday morning in South Fort Worth when two people were found fatally shot outside their home on Buffalo Springs Drive. The victims' identities have not been released.

According to eyewitnesses and police reports, 35-year-old Cary Joseph Heath, a teacher at Permenter Middle School in Cedar Hill, is believed to be responsible for the double murder. Heath was arrested on Monday afternoon after being taken into custody by Fort Worth police.

Heath's arrest came as a surprise to parents and students at Permenter Middle School, where he taught eighth-grade science. Prior to his teaching career, Heath served 13 years in the U.S. Air Force.

Police initially received a report of a robbery at around 4 am on Sunday, but upon arrival, they discovered the bodies of the two victims outside the residence. A witness reported hearing gunshots and seeing shell casings from an assault rifle near the scene.

Cary Heath has been charged with capital murder and is currently being held at the Fort Worth jail on a $1 million bond. He has also been placed on administrative leave by the Cedar Hill Independent School District.

The motive behind the shooting remains unclear, and authorities are still investigating the circumstances surrounding the crime. Parents at Permenter Middle School expressed concern about having a suspect capable of such violence working among children every day.

As the investigation continues, residents and community members are left grappling with the senseless tragedy that unfolded in their neighborhood.
details.ground_truth: Cary Heath was arrested Monday at the Texas middle school where he teaches eighth-grade science a day after police say he murdered two of his neighbors, NBC DFW reports. **Vanderbilt University Renames Confederate Memorial Hall**

In a long-awaited decision, Vanderbilt University has announced that it will rename its Confederate Memorial Hall to simply "Memorial Hall". The move comes after 14 years of debate and controversy surrounding the name.

The university's Chancellor Nicholas Zeppos stated in an interview with The Tennessean that he was pleased with the outcome, saying "You can memorialize without taking sides." He also emphasized that the change is not about erasing history but rather acknowledging the harm caused by symbols associated with racism.

To facilitate this change, Vanderbilt raised $1.2 million from anonymous donors to repay the original donation made by the United Daughters of the Confederacy (UDC) back in 1933. This amount matches the current value of the original gift.

This development follows similar efforts across Tennessee universities to address their own histories tied to slavery and white supremacy. Middle Tennessee State University recently sought permission to remove Nathan Bedford Forrest's bust from campus due to his involvement with the Ku Klux Klan.

Zeppos' statement reflects growing national sentiment against public displays honoring the Confederacy or related figures like General Forrest. In June, the Southern Baptist Convention voted to urge congregations to stop displaying the Confederate flag.

Critics argue that removing such names and imagery does more harm than good as they claim these are part of American heritage. However, supporters see them as painful reminders of systemic oppression and racial violence.

As for other developments:

*   **Middle Tennessee State University**: A proposal to remove Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest's bust from campus faces opposition.
*   **Tennessee Historical Commission**: It must approve any changes to historical markers or monuments under new state law.
*   **Charleston Church Shooting**: Following last year's tragedy, there have been renewed calls to remove Confederate flags and symbols nationwide.

Overall, Vanderbilt's decision marks another step towards re-evaluating America's complex past and addressing ongoing issues of diversity and inclusion on college campuses.
details.ground_truth: In an attempt to bury a relic of its past, Vanderbilt University announced Monday that it will pay more than $1 million to remove the word "Confederate" from one of its dorms, the Tennessean reports. Chancellor Nicholas S. Zeppos called the inscription on Confederate Memorial Hall "a reminder of racism, slavery and a very, very bloody Civil War." The Nashville university's efforts to change the name in 2002 were halted when the United Daughters of the Confederacy sued. The group’s $50,000 donation in 1933 helped build the dorm. A state appeals court ruled the building could be renamed Memorial Hall only after Vanderbilt gave the United Daughters back their money—$1.2 million in today’s dollars. The university has the cash, thanks to a raft of anonymous contributors who wanted the tie to America’s painful past broken for good. "It's a symbol that is, for many people, deeply offensive and painful," Zeppos told the Tennessean. "And to walk past it or to have to live in that space is really something that I just don't think is acceptable.” Yet tampering with Confederate imagery remains controversial, and a new state law makes it harder to do so, the AP reports. Efforts by Middle Tennessee State University in Murfreesboro to remove the name of Confederate Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest from a building could face a tougher climb under the Tennessee Heritage Protection Act, which now requires a vote of two-thirds of the state’s Historical Commission rather than a simple majority.

**Florida Police Officer Replaces Elderly Woman's Stolen Engagement Ring**

In a heartwarming display of kindness and dedication to justice, Plantation Police Officer Laurie Graber purchased an engagement ring for elderly woman Betty Wagner after her original ring was stolen from her hospital room.

The incident occurred on June 14th when Arthur Wagner reported that his wife's $4,500 diamond engagement ring had been taken while she was being treated at Westside Regional Medical Center in Plantation, Florida. The couple has been married for 67 years, with Arthur purchasing the original ring for $400 back in 1947.

Officer Graber took it upon herself to investigate the case and eventually purchase a replacement ring from JCPenney using her own money. She left the new ring along with a heartfelt note at the nursing station, stating "A promise kept is worth something."

While police are still searching for the thief who stole the original ring, Officer Graber's selfless act has brought some comfort to the Wagners during this difficult time. As Arthur said, "It helped ease my pain... A promise kept is worth something."
details.ground_truth: A classy move by a Florida cop is making headlines: Laurie Graber, an officer in Plantation, got the call for a particularly low-level crime—someone had ripped the engagement ring off the finger of an 87-year-old woman bedridden with Alzheimer's in a hospital, reports Fox News. By the bruises on Betty Wagner's finger, it wasn't an easy job, and no wonder—the ring had been there for 67 years. "I just couldn't imagine what kind of depravity you would have to have to take something off of someone so vulnerable," Graber tells WSVN. Upon leaving the hospital, Graber went to JCPenney and shelled out for a replacement ring with her own money. She brought it back to the nurses' station with a note, reports AOL.com: "It's not much, it's not the same. But 67 years of a promise kept should be recognized." Husband Arthur, who placed the original on his soon-to-be wife's hand in 1946, says the gesture has helped him deal with the theft. (Another Florida officer bought groceries for a mom caught shoplifting.)

**Boston Marathon Bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev Seeks New Trial and Appeals Death Sentence**

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, convicted in 2015 for his role in the Boston Marathon bombing that killed three people and injured over 260 others, is seeking a new trial due to alleged prejudicial media coverage and an unconstitutional death sentence.

Tsarnaev's lawyers argue that he was unable to receive a fair trial in Boston because jurors were exposed to widespread outrage and publicity surrounding the attack through social media and other channels. They claim that even on social media, friends and relatives of potential jurors would have seen posts about the bombings, making it impossible for them to remain impartial.

In addition, Tsarnaev's defense team argues that capital punishment has become "cruel and unusual" under current Supreme Court precedent, citing Justice Stephen Breyer's dissenting opinion in a recent case. However, this argument may be difficult to sustain given the majority opinion in the same case upholding the constitutionality of capital punishment.

The appeal also claims that the judge rejected multiple requests from the defense for a change of venue before the trial began, despite concerns about prejudice against Tsarnaev.

Meanwhile, experts predict that Tsarnaev's fate will take years to reach its conclusion, with some estimates suggesting at least 10 years until any possible execution date. This is due in part to the lengthy appeals process, which can drag out cases for decades.

Only three prisoners sentenced to federal death row since 1970 have been executed, highlighting the rarity of executions carried out by the US government. The vast majority of those awaiting execution are serving sentences related to crimes committed within individual states rather than extreme acts of public violence or domestic terrorism like the Boston Marathon bombing.

As Tsarnaev joins the ranks of 62 inmates on federal death row, many of whom have spent more than two decades waiting for their appeals to conclude, questions arise about the fairness and effectiveness of the justice system when dealing with high-profile cases involving capital punishment.
details.ground_truth: Not a huge surprise: Lawyers for Boston marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev today appealed his death-penalty conviction, arguing that "continuous and unrelenting publicity" biased jurors and made a fair trial in Boston impossible, NBC News reports. "Put simply, prejudicial media coverage, events, and environment saturated greater Boston, including the social networks of actual trial jurors, and made it an improper venue for the trial of this case," say the papers. The lawyers want another trial at a new location, the AP reports. Earlier this year, the Guardian reminded us that Tsarnaev's appeals will likely delay his punishment for "at least a decade." The April 15, 2013, bomb strike in Boston left three dead and more than 200 maimed or injured.

**$8 Billion Merger to Create Global Derivatives Giant**

In a major development in the financial industry, IntercontinentalExchange (ICE) is set to acquire NYSE Euronext for approximately $33 per share, or around $8 billion. The deal would create a global derivatives giant with operations spanning 14 stock and futures exchanges and five clearing houses.

The merger marks a significant shift towards electronic trading over traditional "open outcry" floor trading, which has dominated financial markets for centuries. ICE's focus on commodities such as oil, natural gas, and cotton complements NYSE Euronext's expertise in stocks and options, creating a powerful combination that could drive growth and efficiency in the market.

NYSE Euronext's businesses have been struggling due to declining volumes in stock trading, but its derivatives business remains strong. In contrast, ICE has seen steady growth and boasts some of the highest profit margins in the industry.

Regulatory approval will be crucial for the deal to go through, particularly given concerns about antitrust issues. However, analysts believe that this potential merger may pose fewer problems than previous attempts at consolidation between US-based companies.

If approved by regulators and shareholders, the combined company would become the largest exchange operator globally, serving buyers and sellers across multiple asset classes. This move highlights the growing importance of derivatives trading in today's financial landscape, eclipsing even equities trading in terms of volume and revenue.

Shareholders are optimistic about the prospects of the merged entity, with NYSE Euronext shares rising more than 21% after reports emerged of the talks. With regulatory hurdles still ahead, investors await further developments on what promises to be a transformative transaction in the world of finance.
details.ground_truth: InterContinentalExchange Inc. has agreed to buy NYSE Euronext, the company that owns the New York Stock Exchange, for $8.2 billion, the two companies announced this morning. ICE, an Atlanta-based commodity exchange, says it intends to leave the NYSE's branding alone, and would explore an IPO for Euronext, spinning it off into a continental European entity, the Wall Street Journal reports. It will pay $33.12 a share for the elder exchange, or about a 37% premium on yesterday's close. You might remember ICE from its last attempt to buy the NYSE, which failed thanks to antitrust concerns from regulators. While the 12-year-old company may lack the name recognition of the iconic NYSE, it's much larger in terms of market capitalization, at $9.3 billion to NYSE Euronext's $5.8 billion—a sign, the New York Times observes, of how completely commodity trading has outpaced stock trading in relevance.

**Academy Awards Organization Takes Steps to Increase Diversity**

In response to growing criticism and concerns about its lack of diversity, the Academy Of Motion Pictures Arts And Science has taken significant steps towards increasing representation within its membership ranks.

The organization, responsible for awarding the Oscars, sent out 683 new invitations to film industry professionals on Wednesday, marking an unprecedented move in its history. The list includes almost half women (49%) and 41% people of color, representing a major overhaul of the Academy's demographics.

Among those invited are numerous high-profile directors from around the world, including Catherine Breillat, Park Chan-wook, Lucrecia Martel, and Abbas Kiarostami, as well as notable actors such as Idris Elba, Michael B. Jordan, Regina King, and Ice Cube.

This effort comes after years of controversy surrounding the #OscarsSoWhite movement, which was sparked by April Reign's hashtag campaign following consecutive all-white acting Oscar nominations in 2015 and earlier this year. Spike Lee and Jada Pinkett Smith also joined the conversation, prompting the Academy to commit to doubling the number of women and people of color among its members by 2020.

Wednesday marked the first opportunity for the Academy to work toward achieving that goal, with the release of their latest invitation list being hailed as the largest and most diverse class yet. This development is seen as a positive step forward in addressing long-standing issues of exclusion and underrepresentation within the film industry.

With these changes, the Academy aims to create a more inclusive environment that reflects the global nature of cinema. As it continues to evolve, the organization may be able to better represent the rich tapestry of voices and perspectives found in modern filmmaking.
details.ground_truth: Apparently still smarting from some of Chris Rock's Oscars barbs, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences invited 683 people—many of them women and minorities—to join in an unprecedented move Wednesday, Reuters reports. The voting group behind the Oscars is largely old, white, and male and was lambasted this year with the hashtag #OscarsSoWhite after two years in a row of all-white acting nominees. In response, the academy is attempting to—as the AV Club puts it—" add seemingly goddamn everyone it had, for one reason or another, forgotten to invite into its membership.” The actors, directors, and others invited Wednesday include Idris Elba, Eva Mendes, Oscar Isaac, John Boyega, Ice Cube, Greta Gerqig, Michael B. Jordan, Vivica A. Fox, the Wachowskis, James Wan, Luis Guzmán, Kate Beckinsale, Park Chan-wook, James Hong, Michelle Rodriguez, and not one, not two, but three Wayans brothers. Of the new invitees, 46% are women and 41% are people of color. If all 683 accept their invite, women would account for 27% of the more than 7,000 academy members (up from 25%) and minorities would total 11% (up from 8%). “I'm especially happy to be part of such a diverse group. I actually want to hang out and watch movies with most of the people on this list," Arab-German director Lexi Alexander tells the Los Angeles Times. “To be honest, I cried a few tears when I started to get congratulation tweets in Arabic.” Other invitees took to Twitter to share similar sentiments. “Excited to use my vote to nominate talent that reflects the real world we live in—DIVERSITY," tweets Brie Larson, who won best actress at this year's Oscars.

**Iran Delays Trial of Two American Hikers**

The trial of two American hikers, Shane Bauer and Josh Fattal, has been delayed by Iranian authorities due to the absence of their third companion, Sarah Shourd. The three were arrested in July 2009 while hiking near the Iraqi border with Iran.

According to Iranian judiciary spokesman Qolamhossein Molaei, the delay is necessary because Shourd was released on bail earlier this year after being charged with espionage, but she remains in the United States. Their lawyer, Masoud Shafiei, claims he had not received any notification about the postponement.

This development comes as tensions between Washington and Tehran remain high over Iran's nuclear program. The US government has called for the release of the two remaining hikers, who have denied charges of spying against them.

Shourd, who was released from prison in September, described her experience during an interview. She said that they were unaware of the border when they began camping in Kurdish mountains and did not intend to enter Iran. They were captured by soldiers four days later and taken to Evin Prison.

Their arrest has sparked controversy, with some officials suggesting that they may have intentionally crossed into Iran to create publicity or stir up anti-Iranian sentiment. However, both the State Department and Shourd herself deny these allegations, stating that they were simply lost and unlucky.

Meanwhile, Iran has accused the US of trying to prod it back to talks over its nuclear program through various means, including prisoner releases. In February, President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad suggested a possible prisoner swap involving the two Americans, which could potentially lead to improved relations between the two countries.

However, no concrete progress has been made so far, and the fate of the two hikers remains uncertain. As negotiations continue, many are left wondering if justice will be served in this complex case.
details.ground_truth: The three American hikers detained by Iran weren’t captured in Iraq, says Sarah Shourd: They were beckoned over the border by an armed soldier, she tells the New York Times in an effort to set the WikiLeaks version of the story straight. “We did not actually enter Iran until he gestured to us. We were confused and worried and wanted to go back." In Shourd's fullest account of her ordeal to date, she goes into detail about their fateful overnight camping trip, describing "scores of campfires" near the waterfall they were hiking to—which abutted Iran. “I think we were extremely unlucky,” says Shourd. “I guess I never believed there would be so many hundreds of people close to a border.” Her interview with the Times comes ahead of a court date for her fellow hikers, which was set for Saturday but has been delayed by Iran until Shourd “can return to Iran or,” if she refuses, her case can “be dealt with differently,” said an Iranian official. But her lawyer says the trial should go forward; neither he nor Shourd, he tells Reuters, were notified of the change.

**House Intelligence Committee Votes to Release Controversial Memo**

The House intelligence committee voted on Monday in favor of releasing a classified memo that alleges misconduct by senior FBI officials involved in the Russia investigation. The vote was along party lines, with Republicans supporting its release and Democrats opposing it.

The memo, written by Republican members of the committee, accuses senior FBI officials of abusing their power during the 2016 presidential election campaign. It also claims that the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) used flawed information from a dossier compiled by former British spy Christopher Steele to obtain surveillance warrants against Trump campaign associate Carter Page.

Despite concerns raised by the Department of Justice and Democratic lawmakers about potential national security risks, the White House has signaled support for transparency and public disclosure of the document. President Donald Trump's press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said earlier this week that he favors "full transparency" but no decision will be made until after the panel votes.

Two Republican senators, Lindsey Graham and Susan Collins, have urged caution regarding any further action taken by the president as they believe would undermine Mueller probe into Russian interference in US elections.

Meanwhile, Rep Trey Gowdy had lobbied Devin Nunes to share the memo with both the FBI director before making it public. He stated publicly his belief that the memo should not interfere with special counsel Robert Mueller's ongoing investigation into ties between the Trump campaign and Russia.

White House lawyer Ty Cobb released a statement saying that the administration is committed to transparency and will review the memo carefully before deciding whether to make it public.

This development comes amid escalating tensions over the handling of sensitive documents related to the Russia investigation. The controversy surrounding the memo highlights deep divisions within Congress and raises questions about the balance between secrecy and accountability in government investigations.

Key points:

*   A classified memo alleging misconduct by senior FBI officials may soon become public.
*   The memo was approved for release by the House intelligence committee despite opposition from Democrats.
*   The White House supports full transparency but says no final decision can be made without congressional approval.
*   Some lawmakers are urging caution due to concerns about national security implications.
*   Special Counsel Robert Mueller's investigation remains unaffected at present.
details.ground_truth: It's all up to President Trump now. **Breakthrough in Brain-Computer Interface Technology**

Researchers at UC Berkeley have made significant progress in decoding brain activity to reconstruct visual experiences, including YouTube videos and potentially even dreams and memories. The team used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to record brain patterns while subjects watched YouTube clips. They then developed an algorithm that can read these patterns to recreate video footage.

This is not just a novelty; it has potential applications for people with paralysis or other motor disorders who could use their thoughts to control devices. It may also aid detectives by allowing them to analyze witnesses' recollections more accurately.

However, there are limitations to this technology. For instance, reconstructed images will likely remain blurry due to current technical constraints. Moreover, using such tech in court cases would be complicated because memories often contain inaccuracies.

The researchers believe they're on the right path toward understanding how our brains process visuals. Their next step involves analyzing additional modules within the brain's visual system to improve resolution and accuracy. This requires powerful computers capable of handling vast amounts of data.

While we might still be far from achieving "Jedi mind tricks," scientists continue making strides towards reading minds – albeit indirectly through decoded brain signals. As research advances, so do possibilities for its practical application.
details.ground_truth: Scientists at UC Berkeley have made a major advancement in the field of mind reading, reconstructing YouTube videos based on brain scans from people who’d seen them. Researchers would put subjects into an MRI machine and track their brain activity as they viewed videos. Once they’d build a model of how a subject’s mind processed the video, “we could read brain activity for that subject and run it backward … to try to uncover what the viewer saw,” one study coauthor tells ABC News. Using the scans they were then able to reproduce the videos—though they’re blurry. “This is a major leap,” the co-author says. He thinks the technique could eventually be used to reconstruct dreams or memories, if it turns out the brain processes those things similarly to how it processes movies. “It’s our next line of research.” (More details on how the experiment worked, along with a video, at PC Magazine.)

**Congress in Disarray as Sequester Looms**

As the country prepares for the sequestration cuts set to take effect on Friday, Congress is more focused on renaming NASA's Dryden Flight Research Center after Neil Armstrong than addressing the impending crisis.

The House of Representatives spent nearly half an hour debating and passing H.R. 667, which would rename the center after the late astronaut. The bill was sponsored by Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) and passed with little opposition. However, Democrats pointed out the irony of naming a facility after a hero while simultaneously cutting funding for NASA and other essential programs.

Meanwhile, President Obama has been traveling the country warning about the devastating effects of the sequester, but his efforts seem to be falling on deaf ears. Republicans have adopted a strategy of deliberate idleness, refusing to engage in meaningful negotiations or pass any legislation that might mitigate the impact of the cuts.

In fact, many lawmakers are embracing the idea of doing nothing, citing their own salaries will not be affected by the sequester. Congressional staffers may face furloughs and pay cuts, but members of Congress themselves will continue to receive six-figure salaries despite the looming budget cuts.

Critics argue that this lack of urgency from Congress is staggering, particularly given the significant impacts the sequester will have on national defense, education, healthcare, and other critical areas. Despite these concerns, politicians appear unfazed, even joking about having to order their own coffee during recesses.

The contrast between the seriousness of the situation and the lighthearted attitude of some lawmakers is striking. As one commentator noted, "We survived Vietnam, Watergate, and Disco – what can possibly go wrong?"

Ultimately, it remains unclear how long Congress will maintain its current stance, but for now, it seems they're more concerned with paying tribute to American heroes like Neil Armstrong than finding solutions to the nation's pressing problems.

And Roger Simon has a theory on why: Lawmakers' own salaries aren't getting cut, he explains at Politico. **Netflix Hacker Leaks "Orange Is The New Black" Season 5 Episodes**

A hacker, operating under the handle "The Dark Overlord," has released several episodes from Netflix's hit series "Orange is the new black." According to reports, the stolen content was obtained through an attack on a third-party production vendor in late 2016.

According to Variety and AP sources, the leaked season five episodes were uploaded to Pirate Bay by the anonymous cybercriminal after failing to receive payment for their demands. It appears that this individual or group had previously threatened Netflix with releasing the material unless they received money.

This leak may impact Netflix' subscriber growth as well as its stock price since Orange is among the most popular shows on the platform. details.ground_truth: A hacker going by The Dark Overlord claims to have stolen and released 10 episodes of the new season of Orange Is the New Black more than a month before its official release on Netflix. Variety reports the hacker was demanding an unspecified ransom from Netflix, uploading the first episode of the upcoming fifth season to a file-sharing site Friday as proof. The leak of new Orange is the New Black episodes could hurt Neflix's subscriber numbers and stock price. The FBI is investigating.

That's how Air France flight 447 was found in 2009, using "Bayesian statistics" to measure the probability of the plane being in one place or another. **Syrian Civil War Escalates with Twin Blasts in Damascus**

The Syrian capital city of Damascus was rocked by twin blasts targeting the army command headquarters on Wednesday, sparking hours-long gun battles and a raging fire at the heavily guarded compound. The explosions, which were heard miles away, sent black smoke billowing into the air as witnesses described scenes of chaos.

According to state-run media and eyewitnesses, the blasts occurred just after 7am local time near Omayyad Square, causing widespread destruction and panic among civilians. A car bomb is believed to have been responsible for one of the explosions, while the second blast may have been caused by a rebel attack.

At least two people are reported dead, including Maya Naser, an Iranian correspondent working for Press TV who was killed while reporting live from the scene. Her colleague, Hosein Mortada, the network's Damascus Bureau Chief, was injured in the same incident.

The attacks come amid escalating violence between government forces and rebels fighting against President Bashar al-Assad's regime. Over the past few months, insurgents have increasingly targeted military sites and symbols of power, leading to growing casualties on both sides.

The conflict has claimed nearly 30,000 lives since it began in March 2011, according to activists. World leaders gathered at the United Nations General Assembly this week called for international action to end the bloodshed, but Russia and China vetoed any resolution that would condemn Assad's regime or authorize intervention.

In response to the latest attacks, U.S. President Barack Obama pledged support for Syrians seeking to oust Assad, calling him "a dictator" responsible for massacres. However, prospects for international intervention appear slim, given the deep divisions within the UN Security Council.

As tensions escalate, concerns grow about the humanitarian impact of the crisis, which has already displaced hundreds of thousands of people and left many more without access to basic necessities like food and water. With no clear solution in sight, Syria remains mired in civil war, threatening regional stability and global security.

**Decomposing Body Found in Supermarket Column**

A shocking discovery was made on Saturday at a WinCo Foods supermarket in Lancaster, California, when a decomposing body was found stuck inside a brick column outside the store.

According to investigators from the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department (LASD), the body is believed to be that of Raymundo Rivera, 35-year-old man who had been missing since Monday after leading deputies on a foot chase. The suspect allegedly fell onto the roof of the supermarket and became trapped between two columns, where he remained for five days before his remains were discovered by employees due to a strong odor emanating from the area.

The LASD homicide detectives responded to the scene around 11am on Saturday morning, following reports of a foul smell coming from the pillar. Upon investigation, they confirmed that it was indeed a human body, which appeared to have been there for several days.

Witnesses described seeing the suspect run towards the rooftop during the initial pursuit on Monday evening, but lost sight of him as he disappeared over the edge. It is unclear how long the victim may have survived or what caused their death.

An autopsy has been scheduled to determine the cause of death, although officials believe it could be related to heat exposure given the extreme temperatures in the area.

The incident has left many residents shaken, with some expressing concern about safety measures in place at local businesses. An investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death continues, and anyone with information is encouraged to contact the LASD Homicide Bureau.

In the meantime, the community is mourning the loss of life, while also grappling with the unusual nature of this tragic event. As Lt. John Corina noted, "It's one of those strange cases."
details.ground_truth: A strong smell outside a California supermarket turned out to be someone who had decomposed in one of the store's entrance columns, ABC 7 reports. Police were called Saturday to the WinCo Foods in Lancaster after a plumber, told it was likely a septic problem, helped knock brick from the column and saw a shoe and a leg inside. "It's been over 100 degrees up here every day," says LA County Sheriff's Lt. John Corina. "I can't imagine being inside that column and just baking. It's a strange development, and if he died that way, it's a horrible way to die." Police say the victim may be a man who was stopped for a fake license plate Monday night, NBC Los Angeles reports. He crashed the vehicle, ran away from deputies, and got into the supermarket. The man "ran up the steps where the managers [are]," an eyewitness tells CBS Los Angeles. "And somehow he got on the roof. Last I heard, he got away." From up there, he could have reached the store fascia and descended into the column. Whether he died from the fall or baked inside is unclear; he was found on his feet with an arm stuck behind his head. "I saw some gooey liquid and it smelled really foul ... it was oozing out of the pillar onto the pavement," says a witness. "It smelled like death."

Shannon Egeland, a 43-year-old convicted white-collar criminal, was sentenced to an additional three years and ten months in prison on Wednesday after pleading guilty to conspiracy charges related to an insurance scam. However, prosecutors painted a different picture of Egeland, describing him as a "menace to society" who has spent over two decades committing crimes, including mortgage fraud, theft, and possession of controlled substances.

This is not Egeland's first run-in with the law; he previously pleaded guilty to mortgage fraud charges stemming from the Desert Sun housing scandal in Central Oregon in 2009. His lawyer argued that Egeland's mental health issues and physical disability made this stunt a challenge for him, but Judge Brown rejected these claims.

As part of his punishment, Egeland will receive counseling while incarcerated and be required to undergo a new mental health evaluation upon release. This case serves as a stark reminder of the consequences of attempting to manipulate the justice system through deceitful means.
details.ground_truth: A white-collar crook is facing extra prison time for having his son shoot him in the legs with a 20-gauge shotgun, the BBC reports. **Tesla Autopilot Crash Investigation Update**

A 38-year-old Apple engineer Walter Huang died in a fatal crash involving his Tesla Model X on March 23rd while it was engaged on autopilot mode with its Autopilot system activated. The incident occurred near Mountain View, California.

According to investigators and family members, Huang had complained about issues with the Autopilot system multiple times before the accident. His brother Will stated that he had reported problems seven times prior to the crash, including instances where the car swerved towards barriers without warning. Additionally, Huang's wife told ABC7 News I-Team that her husband had taken their vehicle to the dealership several months ago complaining about the issue.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating the cause of the crash, which involved a concrete barrier on Highway 101. CalTrans has acknowledged that they were aware of previous damage to the barrier but failed to repair it within the required timeframe. In fact, there was another accident at the same location just days earlier, which may have contributed to the severity of the impact.

In response to criticism over safety concerns related to Autopilot, Tesla released a statement highlighting the company's commitment to improving road safety through autonomous technology. According to data from Tesla, drivers using Autopilot are three times less likely to be involved in an accident than those driving manually. However, this statistic does not necessarily apply to situations like the recent crash, where human error or equipment failure can still occur.

As investigations continue into both the Uber and Tesla crashes, regulators and lawmakers will need to weigh the benefits against potential risks associated with self-driving vehicles. While some argue that these technologies hold great promise for reducing accidents and saving lives, others raise valid questions regarding liability, accountability, and public trust.

Key points:

*   A 38-year-old Apple engineer named Walter Huang died after crashing his Tesla Model X into a concrete barrier on Highway 101.
*   Investigators found evidence suggesting Huang had previously complained about issues with the Autopilot system, reporting problems as many as seven times before the accident.
*   Caltrans admitted failing to properly maintain the damaged barrier despite being notified by authorities.
*   Tesla maintains that Autopilot makes roads safer, citing statistics showing reduced accident rates among users.
*   Both the NTSB and CHP are conducting separate investigations into the causes behind the tragic event.
details.ground_truth: The Tesla Model X that slammed into a highway barrier in California last week and killed the 38-year-old Apple engineer at the wheel had been on autopilot at the time of the crash, Tesla confirms in a blog post. But the company says driver Walter Huang "received several visual and one audible hands-on warning earlier in the drive," adding that "the driver’s hands were not detected on the wheel for six seconds prior to the collision." Tesla also laid some blame on state highway officials, asserting that "the reason this crash was so severe is because the crash attenuator, a highway safety barrier which is designed to reduce the impact into a concrete lane divider, had been crushed in a prior accident without being replaced." The fact that the vehicle was on autopilot is likely to be controversial because, as ABC News notes, driver Huang had reportedly been concerned about it. His brother told KGO that Huang had brought his Model X back to the dealership complaining that when he used the feature, the car kept swerving toward the very same barrier that it eventually struck in the fatal collision. The NTSB is investigating the crash, including the fire that broke out after the collision. The accident follows another in Arizona in which a self-driving Uber struck and killed a pedestrian.

**Robin Williams: A Legacy of Joy and Genius**

Comedian Robin Williams passed away on Monday at 63 due to asphyxia from an apparent suicide, according to officials ahead of an official coroner's report.

Williams was widely admired in Hollywood for his edgy comedy style that made him stand out among his peers. However, he had a special impact on people born between 1990s-2000s who grew up watching his movies. He shifted gears in the late 90s by taking roles in family-friendly films like "Aladdin," "Mrs Doubtfire" and "Hook." These performances were not only entertaining but also showed how much he cared about bringing joy to children.

His filmography is full of prestige projects such as "Good Will Hunting" which earned him Oscar nomination number four times. But it was during his early days as a comedian when I first met him. At The Comedy Store, he delivered a performance so electrifying that left me speechless. We talked afterwards over dinner where we discussed fame and its challenges. Despite being aware of what lay ahead with his rising stardom, he seemed confident that he could handle it without losing himself.

However, several months later after our conversation, Mork & Mindy became a huge hit making him a household name overnight. When I ran into him again, this time covering the Washington Post, he couldn't have been more surprised by the attention surrounding him. In fact, he downplayed any concerns saying 'that won't happen.' Little did he know just how true those words would be.

Throughout his career, Williams continued to push boundaries both comedically and dramatically. His versatility led him to take on various characters including dark ones that showcased another side of his talent. Even though some may see these choices as far removed from his roots as a stand-up comic, they demonstrate his willingness to explore different aspects of human experience through art.

In conclusion, Robin Williams' legacy will forever be remembered as someone whose passion for spreading joy knew no bounds. From his humble beginnings as a stand-up comedian to becoming a beloved actor, he touched countless lives with his unique brand of humor and heart. As we reflect on his life and work, let us honor his memory by embracing the same spirit of creativity and generosity that defined him throughout his remarkable journey.
details.ground_truth: After Robin Williams' sudden death, the tributes are rolling in, with many recalling a comic genius grappling with private challenges. A sampling: When it comes to comedy, "there wasn't a faster brain on the planet," writes Tony Hicks in the Contra Costa Times. We'll be hearing "a litany of tributes about one of the great comedians who ever lived. Much of it will be some of the same adjectives used when any great performer dies—especially before their time. But in Williams' case, most of it will be true." Early in his career, "it was clear that Mr. Williams was one of the most explosively, exhaustingly, prodigiously verbal comedians who ever lived," AO Scott writes in the New York Times. And beyond that, "his essential persona as an entertainer combined neediness and generosity, intelligence and kindness, in ways that were charming and often unexpectedly moving." Williams may have gotten his start long before Aladdin, but he gave a "generous and humble" gift to the millennial generation, writes Daniel D'Addario at Salon. "Williams will be remembered for his edgy comedy and for dramatic turns, but for people my age, Williams was our childhood," from Mrs. Doubtfire to Jumanji to Flubber. In the Los Angeles Times, Kenneth Turan recalls a moment when, facing an onslaught of photographers, Williams asked him—in the voice of a fly from a 1950s sci-fi flick—to "help me, Ken. Help me." The experience stuck with him and seems particularly resonant today, he writes.
