**MURDER SUSPECT ON THE RUN IN MONTPELIER**

A murder suspect is still at large in Montpelier after a shooting on Sunday morning left 33-year-old Markus Austin dead outside an apartment complex. Jayveon Caballero, also known as Jayveon "Jay" Caballero or Jayveon Caballero, has been identified as the prime suspect and is wanted for second-degree murder.

According to police, Caballero was involved in an altercation with Austin earlier that night at Gusto's bar (also referred to as Gustos) in Barre. The two men were friends, but had gotten into a fight over something unspecified. Witnesses reported hearing shots fired around 4am near the victim's apartment building.

Caballero allegedly shot and killed Austin during this confrontation. A witness described seeing him flee the scene immediately afterwards. Police have reason to believe he may have boarded a Greyhound bus headed south towards New York City.

An arrest warrant has been issued for Caballero, who is believed to be traveling alone. His girlfriend, Desiree Cary, was arrested early Monday morning on unrelated charges related to a drug investigation. She pleaded not guilty and was released from custody later that day.

The search for Caballero continues, with authorities reaching out to neighboring states for assistance. Anyone with information about his whereabouts should contact Vermont State Police.

This marks the first homicide in nearly a century in Montpelier, which boasts just under 8,000 residents. The city's police chief called it a tragic event that shook the community.

Austin was a former member of the now-defunct Frost Heaves basketball team. Friends and family are mourning his loss, while law enforcement officials remain focused on bringing Caballero to justice.

As the manhunt enters its third day, police urge anyone with tips to come forward and help bring closure to the victims' loved ones.
details.ground_truth: Police in the country's smallest state capital are investigating something that hasn't happened there in living memory: a murder. Police in Vermont say they have issued an arrest warrant for 29-year-old Jayveon Caballero, who is accused of fatally shooting Markus Austin in Montpelier early Sunday after an altercation, the Times Argus reports. Witnesses told investigators that Austin, 33, assaulted Caballero’s girlfriend, Desiree Cary, during the altercation outside a bar in the nearby city of Barre early Sunday. Police say Caballero later confronted Austin outside his apartment and shot him dead. The body was found in the parking lot of Austin's apartment complex. A Vermont State Police spokesman says Caballero, who knew Austin before the shooting, fled the town and probably the state after the shooting, WCAX reports. The police spokesman says Caballero is believed to have boarded a Greyhound bus bound for New York City on Sunday morning, which made numerous stops in other states along the way. Later Sunday, Cary, 22, was arrested on apparently unrelated charges of selling heroin and crack cocaine. With around 7,500 residents, Montpelier has the smallest population of any state capital, the AP notes. Police Chief Anthony Facos says this is the city's first murder since a woman shot her husband in the 1920s.

**Rare Super Blue Blood Moon Total Lunar Eclipse on January 31, 2018**

On January 31, 2018, skywatchers around the world will witness an extraordinary celestial event - a total lunar eclipse that coincides with a "Super Blue Blood Moon." This rare occurrence has not been seen in nearly 152 years.

The moon will be at its closest point to Earth (perigee) and appear about 14% larger than usual, earning it the title of supermoon. Additionally, this is also a blue moon, which occurs when there are two full moons within a single month. To make matters even more spectacular, the moon will pass through the Earth's shadow during the eclipse, turning it reddish-orange, hence the term "blood moon."

This unique alignment can be observed from several locations worldwide, including central Asia, Australia, New Zealand, and parts of North America. The Virtual Telescope Project will provide live coverage of the event, allowing viewers to experience the spectacle remotely.

Here are some key details:

* Date: January 31, 2018
* Time:
	+ UTC: 11:48 am (eclipse begins), 4 pm (best viewing time)
	+ Eastern US: 7 am EST (eclipse begins), 12 pm EST (best viewing time)
	+ Western US: 5 am PST (eclipse begins), 10 am PST (best viewing time)
* Visibility: Central Asia, Australia, New Zealand, eastern Asia, western North America
* Duration: Approximately 77 minutes
* Special notes:
	+ Viewers do not need special glasses or equipment; the eclipse is safe to view with the naked eye.
	+ For optimal photography, use a smartphone or DSLR camera with proper exposure settings.

Don't miss this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to witness the awe-inspiring beauty of our planet's only natural satellite as it undergoes a rare transformation under the light of the sun.
details.ground_truth: Look up at the sky on Jan. 31 and you may witness a sight unseen for 150 years. For the first time since 1866, a total lunar eclipse will occur with the blue moon, or second full moon of the month, which—like the one visible on New Year's Day—will also be a supermoon. Got all that? When the moon is at or near the closest point to Earth in its orbit (aka, a supermoon), it appears 14% bigger and 30% brighter than full moons that occur at the farthest point in the moon's orbit, though the moon will lose brightness as it enters Earth's shadow, according to NASA. Because of the way Earth's atmosphere bends light, the eclipsed moon will take on a reddish hue, something often referred to as a blood moon, making this rare celestial event "a super blue blood moon eclipse," according to the Miami Herald. The next blue moon eclipse won't occur until 2028. The eclipse will last for 3.5 hours, with the total eclipse stretching for 77 minutes, reports Sky & Telescope. Those along the Pacific Rim from Alaska and northwestern Canada to central and eastern Asia, Indonesia, New Zealand, and Australia will get the best view of totality during the middle of the night. However, partial phases of the eclipse should be visible under a clear sky in central North America, western Asia, India, the Middle East and eastern Europe, per Space.com. North American viewers should look up as the moon sets on the morning of Jan. 31, while those on the opposite side of the world should see a partial eclipse as the moon rises. Not in an ideal viewing area? The Virtual Telescope plans to livestream the total eclipse from Australia, which you can watch here, per Quartz. (Bogus glasses damaged a solar eclipse viewer's eyes.)

**Syrian Protests Escalate as US Ambassador Visits Hama**

The situation in Syria continues to deteriorate as protests against President Bashar al-Assad's government intensify across the country. On Friday, over 500,000 people gathered in the city of Hama, which has become a symbol of opposition since the 1982 crackdown on protesters.

US Ambassador Robert Ford visited Hama on Thursday, meeting with local residents and showing support for their cause. The visit was seen as an effort by the State Department to demonstrate its commitment to democracy and human rights in Syria. However, the Syrian government accused the US of interfering in its internal affairs and violating diplomatic protocol by not seeking permission before sending the ambassador to Hama.

Despite the tensions, thousands more protested in cities across Syria, including Homs and Damascus. Activists reported at least 13 deaths nationwide, while Human Rights Watch estimated that up to 20,000 people may have been killed during last month's crackdowns.

In response to the growing unrest, Western diplomats are increasing their involvement in the crisis. French Ambassador Eric Chevallier also visited Hama this week, and several other countries have condemned Assad's regime for its violent suppression of peaceful demonstrations.

Meanwhile, reports emerged of further violence in the city of Hasrata just outside Damascus, where three people were reportedly killed when security forces opened fire on protesters near a mosque. Thousands of civilians have fled Salamiyah after being forced out of their homes by troops, according to activists.

As the death toll rises and international pressure mounts, it remains unclear whether Assad will be able to maintain control or if his regime is nearing collapse. One thing is certain, however - the Syrian people continue to demand change and freedom from what they see as a corrupt and oppressive government.

Key Developments:

* Over 500,000 Syrians protest in Hama, marking largest demonstration yet against Assad's government.
* At least 13 protesters killed nationwide, with estimates suggesting up to 20,000 dead in recent weeks.
* US Ambassador Robert Ford visits Hama, sparking accusations from Syrian government of interference.
* Western diplomats increase involvement in crisis, with France condemning Assad's regime.
* Violence erupts in Hasrata, with three reported fatalities; thousands flee Salamiyah due to troop presence.
details.ground_truth: America's ambassador to Syria visited one of the cities worst-hit by the crackdown against anti-government protesters yesterday, reports CNN. An estimated 500,000 people joined an anti-government rally in the city last Friday. An embassy spokeswoman says the Syrian government was told a delegation would be visiting Hama, although no Syrian "handlers" were taken and officials weren't informed about the ambassador's presence. **Election Security Threats on the Rise Ahead of Midterms**

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) has been at the center of two recent incidents that highlight the growing threat of election security breaches and foreign meddling in US politics.

Initially, it was reported that hackers had attempted to breach the DNC's voter database by creating a fake login page designed to trick users into handing over their usernames and passwords. The incident sparked concerns about the vulnerability of electoral systems and the potential for manipulation ahead of the midterm elections.

However, further investigation revealed that what appeared to be a sophisticated hacking attempt was actually an unauthorized "simulated phishing test" conducted without the knowledge or consent of the DNC.

Despite this development, experts warn that the cyber age has changed elections forever, making many systems vulnerable to manipulation. Bob Lord, chief security officer for the DNC, described the party's voter file as its most sensitive information, emphasizing the need for vigilance against future attacks.

Recent reports have also highlighted continued influence operations by Russia and other countries using social media, as well as efforts to breach think tanks and government organizations. Microsoft detected attempts by Russian intelligence-linked hackers to target the Senate and conservative think tanks through fake websites.

Facebook has also identified disinformation campaigns aimed at disrupting the midterms and targeting people around the world. As the country heads towards the November elections, political groups and government organizations are on high alert for new hacks and foreign meddling.

Experts like Rob Joyce, former White House cybersecurity coordinator, note that the focus has shifted from stealing secrets to imposing national power through cyber means. This shift underscores the evolving nature of threats to election security and highlights the need for increased vigilance and cooperation between governments, private companies, and civil society to prevent future attacks.
details.ground_truth: The FBI is reportedly investigating a sophisticated—but unsuccessful—attempt to hack into the Democratic National Committee's voter database. The DNC learned of the attempt on Tuesday, CNN reports. The attack, which was detected by a cloud service provider and a security research company, involved a fake login page intended to gather usernames and passwords for a service called Votebuilder, which hosts the DNC's voter database. It's a method called "spearphishing," according to the New York Times. "It was very convincing," Mike Murray of the cybersecurity firm Lookout tells CNN, adding that it would be tough to tell the real page from the fake one, even if they were side-by-side. The fake login page was ultimately removed by the cloud hosting company DigitalOcean. The company's chief security officer says the threat was identified before the attack was launched. "We see no evidence that any sensitive data was stolen," he says. A DNC official tells the Times that it is not clear who the hackers were in this case. But, the paper recalls, a 2016 hack of the DNC was ultimately traced to Russia. This latest attempt, DNC Chief Security Officer Bob Lord tells the Times, "is further proof that there are constant threats as we head into midterm elections and we must remain vigilant in order to prevent future attacks." Earlier this week, Microsoft reported that it had uncovered new Russian hacking attempts targeting conservative organizations in the US.

**Boston Marathon Bombing Aftermath**

Tragedy struck Boston on Monday when two explosions rocked the finish line at the 117th annual Boston Marathon, killing three people and injuring hundreds more. The victims have been identified as Martin Richard, an 8-year-old boy from Dorchester; Krystle Campbell, a 29-year-old restaurant manager from Medford; and Lelisa Desisa's friend, a Chinese university student whose name has not yet been released pending family approval.

The bombings sent shockwaves through the city, with many residents struggling to come to terms with the senseless violence. A vigil was held for Martin Richard in his neighborhood, where hundreds gathered to pay their respects. His father, Bill Richard, released a statement expressing grief and gratitude for the outpouring of support.

In another tragic twist, a Medford family received devastating news that their daughter, Krystle Campbell, had died from her injuries after being told she would survive. Her parents are still grappling with the loss.

As investigators work tirelessly to identify those responsible, Mayor Thomas Menino vowed that Boston will "not be intimidated" by terrorism. FBI officials also assured the public that there were no known additional threats.

Despite the trauma, the city is coming together to heal and move forward. Residents, runners, and visitors alike are showing solidarity and resilience in the face of evil. President Obama praised first responders and the community's response, saying it defines who Americans are.

details.ground_truth: Another fatality in the Boston bombings has been identified: The family of 29-year-old Krystle Campbell says she was killed as she and a friend were cheering on another friend who was racing, reports WCVB. **Global Obesity Epidemic Reaches Alarming Proportions**

A recent study published in The Lancet has revealed that obesity is a growing concern worldwide, affecting nearly 30% of the global population, or approximately 2.1 billion adults. This staggering number represents an increase of over 50% since 1980 and highlights the alarming rate at which this public health issue is spreading.

The United States leads the world in obesity rates, with around 87 million people affected, but it's far from being alone. Other countries such as Tonga, Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Libya, Algeria, Egypt, and Mexico also have high obesity rates, often exceeding 20%. In fact, no country has managed to reduce its obesity rate over the past three decades.

Obesity affects not only developed nations but also developing ones, where two-thirds of obese individuals reside. The Middle East region stands out for having some of the highest obesity rates globally, particularly among women. For example, in Bahrain, more than half of adult men are now classified as overweight or obese.

Children are also increasingly falling victim to obesity, with rates rising by almost 50% between 1998 and 2013. Younger generations are facing higher risks due to sedentary lifestyles and easy access to cheap, high-calorie foods.

According to researchers, food availability and affordability play significant roles in fueling the epidemic. "We need to remind ourselves that obesity is not just a cosmetic issue; it's a major risk factor for morbidity and mortality," said Dr. Ali Mokdad, co-author of the report.

To combat this crisis, experts recommend addressing lifestyle changes through education, policy reforms, and increased physical activity opportunities. A World Health Organization (WHO) commission was launched earlier this year to explore solutions to address childhood obesity specifically.

As the global community grapples with this pressing challenge, awareness about the causes and consequences of obesity must be raised. Only then can we hope to stem the tide of this rapidly escalating problem and ensure healthier futures for future generations.

Key statistics:

* Approximately 2.1 billion adults worldwide suffer from obesity or excess weight.
* No country has reduced its obesity rate over the last 33 years.
* Two-thirds of obese individuals live in developing countries.
* Children under 18 account for nearly 40% of new cases each year.
* Overweight/obese populations exceed 10% in every single country studied.

Sources:
USA Today, Reuters, WHO reports.
details.ground_truth: There are more obese or overweight people in the world today than there were people of any weight in 1935, the most comprehensive look at worldwide obesity in decades warns. The 188-country study found that there are 2.1 billion overweight or obese people in the world, making up around 30% of the world's population, up from 20% in 1980, USA Today reports. Not a single country has recorded a decline in obesity over the last 30 years. "We hoped there would be some examples of success that you could latch onto," a study co-author says. "But there's a complete lack of success stories in bringing down obesity." The study published in British medical journal the Lancet found that the Middle East and north Africa had seen the biggest weight gains, though the US still has the largest number of obese people, with 87 million of the world's 671 million obese people, reports Reuters. Other countries, however, have even higher obesity rates, including Tonga, where more than 50% of all adults are obese. "Two-thirds of the obese population actually resides in developing countries," says one of the researchers; they warn that obesity rates are rising among rich and poor countries, men and women, and adults and children alike.

**Egypt's Parliamentary Elections and Mubarak Trial**

In Egypt, Egyptians voted in the final round of parliamentary elections on January 3rd as prosecutors presented their case against former president Hosni Mubarak. The Muslim Brotherhood is expected to maintain its lead after three rounds of voting.

The election results are uncertain due to unclear rules for calculating seats won by each party. However, analysts predict that Islamist group will secure a majority in parliament. In the first two rounds, it secured nearly half of available seats.

Meanwhile, the trial of ousted Egyptian leader continued with chief prosecutor Mustafa Suleiman delivering scathing critique of his rule. He accused him of imposing "tyrannical" rule and devoting last decade to ensure son Gamal would succeed him. NEWLINE_CHAR NEWLINE_CHAR Prosecutors also charged Mubarak with corruption charges related to sale of state-owned assets during his tenure. details.ground_truth: The final round of voting began in Egypt today, and it looks like the Muslim Brotherhood could walk off with a controlling majority of seats in Parliament's lower house. The Muslim Brotherhood's Freedom and Justice Party, the country's mainstream Islamist party, had already won a high percentage of the seats awarded in the first and second rounds of voting. Two of the nine provinces voting today are Brotherhood strongholds, where some of the party's most well-known candidates are running, the New York Times reports. A plurality, not a majority, was originally predicted for the Freedom and Justice Party. A majority would allow the party to govern alone, but the Brotherhood has repeatedly said it plans to form a coalition government, and has aligned itself with more liberal parties rather than the ultraconservative Salafis, who are in second place with up to 25% of the seats so far. Also today, prosecutors began presenting their case against former Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, Bloomberg notes. His trial resumed last week after a two-month break; state TV today showed Mubarak being carried to and from the courtroom on a gurney. "He deserves an end of humiliation and indignity," said the chief prosecutor, according to the AP.

**LOCAL NEWS SUMMARY**

A bizarre incident occurred in Mendon on Wednesday evening when a car was suspended from a telephone pole's guy wire after its driver reacted too quickly to GPS directions.

According to State Police, Nabila Altahan was driving her Toyota Corolla westbound on Route 4 with a passenger when she received sudden turn-around instructions from her GPS device. The vehicle had passed its intended destination and the GPS system mistakenly directed Altahan to make an immediate U-turn.

In response to the incorrect direction, Altahan took evasive action by leaving the road, resulting in her car becoming lodged on the support cable of a nearby telephone pole across from Sugar & Spice Restaurant. Fortunately, neither Altahan nor her passenger were injured during the ordeal.

Eyewitnesses reported that Altahan jumped out of the car as it hung precariously from the pole, prompting a swift response from local authorities. State police and Rutland City Fire Department personnel arrived at the scene shortly thereafter.

The incident serves as a reminder for drivers to exercise caution when following GPS navigation systems, especially if they are not familiar with their surroundings or have made errors while inputting destinations into the device.

This unusual accident highlights the importance of verifying information provided by technology before taking any actions behind the wheel. It also underscores the need for situational awareness and responsible decision-making among motorists.

No further details regarding potential charges against Altahan or damage assessments related to the incident could be found in available reports. However, this remarkable story will undoubtedly leave readers questioning the reliability of relying solely on GPS guidance without proper verification.
details.ground_truth: Police in Vermont say a car ended up almost vertical when the driver swerved quickly in response to her GPS ordering her to "turn around." The car was suspended almost vertically on guide wires attached to a utility pole (see a photo here) in Mendon on Wednesday night, reports the AP. Police say 30-year-old Nabila Altahan of Dorchester, Mass., was headed west on US Route 4 when she passed her intended destination and reacted quickly to the instructions, leaving the road at a significant enough speed to propel the vehicle up the wires. She wasn't injured. (This driver followed her GPS into a lake.)
